$comment: Content for Equal & Confident (node g50, ages 18-22, Chapter 6): NEW v2 build to GDD 50 (mechanic-embodying),
taking the gender-equality & allyship work of the teen years into adult arenas where it bites: the seminar
room, the internship, the first job, public life (Thread E · Gender & Respect, Leadership & Confidence domain).
Reworks the old ModesEngine build onto the shared v2 engine. 84 researched, India-grounded scenarios across
claim-your-voice → lead-the-room → spot-counter-bias → be-the-ally → equality-lifts-everyone → tools-and-help,
each encoded as one of the shared v2 play actions (branch / strike-rewrite / sort / reflect / role-play / spot
/ match): no binary "tap the right card". Lead: branch (your move), strike-rewrite (bust the myth), role-play
(say the line). Five modes: claim your voice (speak, contribute, don't be talked over), lead the room
(leadership without a title), spot & counter bias (interruptions, the 'bossy' double-bind, office housework;
UN&RE), be the ally (active allyship across genders), tools & help. Builds women's confidence and leadership
while engaging men as allies; EQUALITY LIFTS EVERYONE (not zero-sum). Evenhanded, never anti-boy; confidence
framed inclusively. Harassment routes to rights/redress (POSH, covered in g51) and help (181, POSH Internal
Committees). India: women sharply under-represented in workforce and leadership; campus and workplace bias and
harassment are real. Builds on g33 (Lead the Way) & g26 (Equalize); pairs g51; feeds Chapters 7-8 (g55, g62).
title: Equal & Confident
greet: Hey, it’s Lensy. Equality now hits the classroom, internship and first job. Claim your voice, lead without a title, spot bias, be an ally. Equality lifts all.

badge.title: Equal & Confident 🌟
badge.blurb: You can claim your voice, lead without a title, spot and counter the everyday bias, and be a real ally, because equality isn’t zero-sum, it lifts everyone. 🤝

helpLine: Speaking up is yours to claim. Harassment is never your fault. In India, harassment can go to a POSH Internal Committee, or call the Women Helpline 181.
reassure: Being boxed in by bias is no flaw in you. Harassment is never your fault: a POSH Internal Committee or the Women Helpline 181 can help. You belong here. 🌟

scenarios.hook: "If I haven't got a fully-formed point, I shouldn't speak up."

myth.un: I shouldn't speak unless my point is fully formed.
myth.re: Your half-formed thought is often as valuable as anyone's; you belong in the conversation.
myth.why: Plenty of people speak freely with rougher ideas.

scenarios.relearn: You belong in the conversation; a half-formed thought is still worth voicing.

scenarios.hook: You're mid-point in a seminar, making a case about the survey data.
scenarios.setup: The professor is taking notes as you speak.

steps.prompt: A classmate cuts in: "Sorry, but I think the real issue is the budget."

options.text: "I'd like to finish my point, thanks."
options.then: She stops. "Oh, of course. Please finish."

options.text: "Oh, sorry. Go on, go on."
options.then: She carries on about the budget. Your point is left hanging.

options.text: "It's okay. My point wasn't that important."
options.then: She smiles and keeps going. The professor writes nothing down.

options.text: "Excuse me, don't interrupt me like that."
options.then: She bristles. "I only added a thought." Eyes turn to you.

steps.why: Calmly finishing your point takes back the floor without a fight.

steps.prompt: Ten minutes later, the professor says: "Let's recap. What were the main points so far?"

options.text: "Mine was the survey. It shapes the budget too."
options.then: The professor nods and writes "survey" on the board.

options.text: "The budget, mainly. That was the big one."
options.then: The professor writes "budget". Your point isn't on the board.

options.text: "I don't remember. Ask the others."
options.then: Someone else answers. Your point is left off the list.

options.text: "Mine was minor. It doesn't need to go up."
options.then: The professor nods and moves on to the next point.

steps.why: Naming your own point in the recap keeps it on the record.

steps.prompt: After class, the classmate says: "I didn't realise I cut you off."

options.text: "Honestly, I thought you did it on purpose."
options.then: She frowns. "No! Why would you think that?"

options.text: "It's fine. Don't worry about it."
options.then: She nods, relieved. The habit has no reason to change.

options.text: "You always do that. I'm tired of it."
options.then: She flushes. "That's a bit harsh."

options.text: "No worries. Let's each finish our points."
options.then: She grins. "Deal. I'll wait for you to finish."

steps.why: A friendly agreement helps the habit change without a row.

scenarios.relearn: You can calmly reclaim the floor when you're talked over.

scenarios.hook: You're in a packed lecture with a question that you fear will sound stupid.

steps.prompt: The lecturer asks if there are any questions. What do you do?

options.text: Whisper it to your neighbour instead
options.then: Your neighbour shrugs. "No idea either." Neither of you asks.

options.text: Wait and look it up after class
options.then: You find an answer online. The lecturer's version stays unheard.

options.text: Ask it plainly, since others may be wondering too
options.then: Two students nod. The lecturer says, "Let me explain that again."

options.text: Stay silent, since everyone else seems to follow
options.then: The lecture moves on. The question sits unanswered in your notebook.

steps.why: Others are often wondering too, and asking helps the whole room.

steps.prompt: A classmate says she never asks in class, worried people will think she doesn't belong. What do you say?

options.text: "Then just stop worrying about it."
options.then: She nods, but the worry doesn't go anywhere.

options.text: "Me too sometimes. Try one a week. It gets easier."
options.then: She smiles. "One a week. I can try that."

options.text: "Copy my notes and skip the questions, then."
options.then: She takes the notes gratefully. Her questions stay unasked.

options.text: "Email the lecturer instead, every single time."
options.then: She agrees. The class never hears her questions.

steps.why: Sharing your own worry and starting small helps others try.

steps.prompt: Before exams, the lecturer's office hours are open and you still have a doubt. What do you do?

options.text: Wait to see if it comes up in revision
options.then: It doesn't come up. The doubt travels into the exam hall.

options.text: Skip it and ask a friend instead
options.then: Your friend gives a guess. You're still not sure.

options.text: Go, with the specific question written down
options.then: The lecturer reads it and explains it in five minutes. You leave lighter.

options.text: Go, but only say you feel a bit lost
options.then: The lecturer smiles and says, "Lost where?" You can't say.

steps.why: A specific question gets a specific answer.

scenarios.debrief: The question you're afraid to ask is often the one the whole room needs.
scenarios.relearn: Ask the question you're afraid of; others usually share it.

scenarios.hook: "I should soften everything I say with 'sorry' and 'just'."

myth.un: I should pad everything with 'sorry' and 'just'.
myth.re: You can state your point directly; over-apologising shrinks your message.
myth.why: Confident, clear phrasing carries your idea further.

scenarios.relearn: State your point directly; over-apologising shrinks your message.

scenarios.hook: You want to contribute an idea in a meeting full of louder voices.
scenarios.setup: The discussion is fast and the gaps are short.

steps.prompt: The chair asks: "Any other ideas before we move on?"

options.text: "I've got an idea I'd like to add here."
options.then: The chair nods. "Go ahead. We're listening."

options.text: "No, I think the others covered it."
options.then: The chair nods and moves on. Your idea stays inside.

options.text: "Hold on, everyone! Please stop talking, all of you."
options.then: The room goes quiet, surprised. Now everyone is looking at you, not at your idea.

options.text: "Oh, it's probably nothing. Maybe later."
options.then: "Later" never comes. The meeting ends.

steps.why: Step in clearly. The perfect gap never comes.

steps.prompt: At the next meeting, as you start an idea, a louder colleague says: "We're short on time. Keep it quick."

options.text: "I need as long as I need, actually."
options.then: The room groans. You get three minutes and a cold audience.

options.text: "Two minutes. It's a small pilot."
options.then: She checks her watch. "Fine. Go on."

options.text: "Never mind then. Sorry for asking."
options.then: She smiles, relieved. Your idea goes unspoken again.

options.text: "Fine. I'll send it by email instead."
options.then: She nods. The email joins forty others.

steps.why: Saying how long you need, and then using it, keeps the floor.

steps.prompt: The chair asks: "Who wants to take the next step on the open ideas?"

options.text: "I'll do it if nobody else volunteers."
options.then: Silence. Then someone else speaks first.

options.text: "I can take it. I'll share a plan by Friday."
options.then: The chair writes your name down. "Friday it is."

options.text: "Maybe someone else. I'm not sure I'm the one."
options.then: Someone else takes it, and does it differently.

options.text: "The loudest person should handle it."
options.then: A few laughs. The loudest person takes it.

steps.why: Stepping in includes taking the next step.

scenarios.relearn: Step in clearly to add your idea; don't wait for a perfect gap.

scenarios.hook: Sort: claims your voice, or shrinks it?

items.text: Going quiet when one person frowns

scenarios.relearn: Stating ideas plainly, finishing your point and re-tabling claims your voice; trailing off and yielding shrinks it.

scenarios.hook: You're nervous about speaking, but you have something worth saying.

steps.prompt: A meeting is wrapping up and your point is still unsaid. What do you do?

options.text: Speak now, even with your nerves
options.then: Your voice shakes for a second. Then the room listens and it settles.

options.text: Wait until you feel ready to say it
options.then: The meeting ends. The point is still in your head.

options.text: Send it later by email instead
options.then: You send it that evening. One reply reads: "That would have helped in the room."

options.text: Whisper it to the colleague beside you
options.then: She whispers: "You should tell everyone." The meeting has just ended.

steps.why: Confidence grows by speaking, not by waiting to feel ready.

steps.prompt: Next week you have another chance to speak, and your hands are cold. What do you do?

options.text: Start with one short sentence and go on
options.then: The first sentence is the hardest. The second is easier.

options.text: Skip this one and save your courage
options.then: The chance passes. Your hands warm up when it's too late.

options.text: Ask someone else to say it for you
options.then: They say it well. You wonder why you didn't.

options.text: Write a full script and read it out word for word
options.then: You read it stiffly. The room hears the script, not you.

steps.why: Starting small makes speaking easier each time.

steps.prompt: A month later, a friend says she's too nervous to speak up at all. What do you tell her?

options.text: "Some people are just naturally shy. Don't force it."
options.then: She nods with relief. She also shrinks a little.

options.text: "Start small. Speak before you feel ready."
options.then: She laughs. "That's it? Okay. I'll try tomorrow."

options.text: "Just don't think about it so much, yaar."
options.then: She sighs. "I wish it were that easy."

options.text: "Wait until you feel confident. It will come."
options.then: She nods. The confident day doesn't arrive.

steps.why: Courage grows by doing, even a little.

scenarios.debrief: Confidence is built by speaking before you feel ready, not after.
scenarios.relearn: Speak even when nervous; confidence grows by doing.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: your voice and ideas belong in every room you're in. Let that settle?
scenarios.affirm: You belong in the room and your voice counts; never let anyone make you doubt that.
scenarios.relearn: Your voice and ideas belong in every room you're in.

scenarios.hook: "If a woman is quiet in meetings, she has nothing to add."

myth.un: If a woman's quiet in meetings, she has nothing to add.
myth.re: Many capable people are talked over or hold back; the room should make space, not assume emptiness.
myth.why: Silence is often the room's fault, not the person's.

scenarios.relearn: Many capable people are talked over; the room should make space, not assume they have nothing.

scenarios.hook: A quieter teammate, Priya, keeps getting cut off when she starts to speak.
scenarios.setup: She has just started speaking again.

steps.prompt: A louder teammate cuts in: "Sorry, let me just add something first."

options.text: "Hang on. Priya was mid-point. Let's hear her."
options.then: He pauses. "Oh, sorry, Priya. Go on."

options.text: "Priya, could you speak up a bit? We can't hear you."
options.then: Priya flushes. She speaks louder, and is talked over again.

options.text: "Go ahead. Priya can wait a minute."
options.then: He talks for three minutes. Priya gives up.

options.text: "Both of you, please just calm down now."
options.then: Priya stiffens. She wasn't shouting.

steps.why: Opening space for a teammate is a simple and kind act.

steps.prompt: Later, Priya says: "I never know when to jump in. Any tips?"

options.text: "Just speak louder and faster than the others."
options.then: She winces. "That's not me."

options.text: "Wait for a pause. There will be one, eventually."
options.then: She nods. There's never a pause in that room.

options.text: "Try a short first sentence. I'll help make space."
options.then: She smiles. "A short first line. Okay. And you'll help?"

options.text: "I'll speak for you whenever you get stuck."
options.then: She smiles, unsure. She's now relying on you to speak.

steps.why: A short first line plus a friend who makes space works.

steps.prompt: At the next meeting, someone new cuts in on Priya and says: "Quick one from me first."

options.text: "Anyway, shall we move on to the next item?"
options.then: Everyone relaxes. Priya's point never returns.

options.text: "One sec. Priya, you were saying?"
options.then: He stops. Priya picks up her point and finishes it.

options.text: "Go on, then. Priya, you can add after."
options.then: He talks on. By the time he stops, Priya has let it go.

options.text: "Priya, are you going to let him do that?"
options.then: Priya flushes. "I... never mind." She looks at her notes.

steps.why: Doing it again, and again, makes it the room's habit.

scenarios.relearn: Open space for a teammate who keeps getting cut off.

scenarios.hook: Your idea is brushed aside, then praised when a louder colleague, Vikas, repeats it.

steps.prompt: The manager loves it and thanks Vikas. What do you do?

options.text: Call Vikas a thief in front of the team
options.then: Vikas bristles. "I didn't steal anything." Everyone goes silent.

options.text: Calmly say it was your idea, and build on it
options.then: The room turns to you. "Right, you did say that. Go on."

options.text: Agree it's a great idea and move on
options.then: The team nods along. The idea is now Vikas's.

options.text: Stay quiet and seethe inside
options.then: The meeting moves on. Vikas takes the next action item.

steps.why: You can reclaim credit calmly, by saying it was yours and building on it.

steps.prompt: Later, Vikas says: "Great idea. I'm taking it to the director." What do you say?

options.text: "Fine, but I'll tell the director you copied me."
options.then: His face hardens. "That's not fair. I built on it."

options.text: "Go ahead. It doesn't matter who presents."
options.then: He grins. The director hears only his name.

options.text: "It started as mine. Let's present it together."
options.then: Vikas pauses. "Fair. Let's do it together, then."

options.text: "Do what you like. I won't help with it."
options.then: He shrugs. You are now out of the project entirely.

steps.why: Claiming your part, and offering to share, keeps it fair and open.

steps.prompt: Before the next meeting, you have another idea. What do you do?

options.text: Keep it to yourself this time
options.then: You go to the meeting with nothing to say.

options.text: Share it in writing first, then say it aloud
options.then: The message has your name and time on it. The room hears it, too.

options.text: Wait for a quiet moment with the manager
options.then: The quiet moment doesn't arrive. The idea goes stale.

options.text: Hand it to Vikas, since he's louder
options.then: He presents it well. It's still his.

steps.why: Putting it in writing and saying it aloud makes it clearly yours.

scenarios.debrief: You can reclaim credit for your idea gracefully, without conflict.
scenarios.relearn: If your idea is re-credited, calmly note it was yours and build on it.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: speaking up gets easier each time you do it. Worth practising?
scenarios.affirm: Each time you use your voice, the next time gets a little easier; it's a practice.
scenarios.relearn: Speaking up gets easier each time you practise it.

scenarios.hook: You spot a role you want, but you don't meet every single requirement.

steps.prompt: The deadline is three days away. What do you do?

options.text: Wait to see whether a stronger person applies
options.then: You wait for news that never comes. On the last evening, you start the form in a rush.

options.text: Ask a friend whether you even qualify
options.then: Your friend says, "Who knows?" The deadline gets closer.

options.text: Apply anyway and show what you do bring
options.then: You start the application that evening. It feels bold, and you're well into it.

options.text: Wait until you've ticked every box
options.then: Three days isn't enough to tick every box. You start the form on the last night anyway.

steps.why: You rarely need to tick every item to apply.

steps.prompt: The form ends with an "anything else to add" box. What do you write?

options.text: Two lines on your strongest relevant work
options.then: Two crisp lines. They show what you've done, not what you haven't.

options.text: An apology for the skill you're missing
options.then: You apologise before anyone asks. The gap is now the first thing they read.

options.text: Nothing, since you're behind on the list
options.then: The box stays empty. The form looks thin.

options.text: Everything you've ever done, in a long list
options.then: The list is three pages. The best part is hard to find.

steps.why: Leading with your strengths shows what you bring.

steps.prompt: On the call, they ask about the skill you lack. What do you say?

options.text: "I haven't used it yet. Here's how I'd learn it."
options.then: The interviewer nods. "That's honest. How soon could you start?"

options.text: "I've done it plenty of times. Don't worry."
options.then: They ask for an example. The room goes quiet.

options.text: "It isn't really important for this role."
options.then: They raise an eyebrow. "We think it is."

options.text: "I'm sorry. I know I'm not fully qualified."
options.then: The interviewer's face goes flat. The call gets shorter.

steps.why: Honesty plus a plan for the gap builds trust.

scenarios.debrief: Plenty of qualified people count themselves out by waiting to tick every box. Apply anyway.
scenarios.relearn: Apply even if you don't meet every requirement; you rarely need all of them.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a confidence-builder, or a confidence-drainer?

items.text: Comparing yourself to the loudest person

scenarios.relearn: Preparing, recalling wins and rehearsing builds confidence; assuming embarrassment, replaying flaws and harsh comparison drains it.

scenarios.hook: "Leadership requires a title or position."

myth.un: Leadership requires a title or position.
myth.re: Leadership is initiative and lifting others; you can lead from any seat.
myth.why: The most useful leadership often has no title.

scenarios.relearn: Leadership is initiative and lifting others; you can lead from any seat.

scenarios.hook: A group project is drifting and no one's taking charge.

steps.prompt: The deadline is ten days away and nobody has a plan. What do you do?

options.text: Propose a simple plan and ask each person to pick a part
options.then: People nod. One asks, "Can I take the slides?"

options.text: Wait for the topper or the class rep to take charge
options.then: Two more days pass, and the group chat stays silent.

options.text: Quietly start doing the whole project yourself
options.then: You work late, and the others relax.

options.text: Post in the chat that someone should take charge
options.then: Three thumbs-up appear, and nobody steps forward.

steps.why: A simple plan with a part for everyone turns drift into movement.

steps.prompt: At the first meeting, one teammate says he'd rather work alone. What do you do?

options.text: Let him work alone, to avoid any trouble
options.then: His part arrives late and doesn't match the rest.

options.text: Insist that he joins every meeting, no exceptions
options.then: He sits through the meetings with his arms folded.

options.text: Quietly give his part to someone keener instead
options.then: He notices, and stops replying in the group chat.

options.text: Ask what he'd like to own, and agree how to share updates
options.then: He picks the research. "Okay. Updates every Friday."

steps.why: Letting him choose a part, with clear check-ins, keeps him in without forcing him.

steps.prompt: Halfway through, two teammates clash over how to write the report. What do you do?

options.text: Pick the side you agree with so it's settled fast
options.then: One teammate feels overruled and does less after that.

options.text: Step back and let them sort it out themselves
options.then: The clash drags on, and the report stalls for two days.

options.text: Bring them together to agree one shared outline
options.then: They argue for ten minutes, then agree on an outline you type up.

options.text: Ask the teacher to decide who is right, please
options.then: The teacher says it's the group's job, and the two stop speaking.

steps.why: Agreeing one shared outline settles the clash and keeps the project moving.

steps.prompt: The deadline is tomorrow and one section is missing. What do you do?

options.text: Write the whole missing section yourself tonight
options.then: You finish at 3 a.m. The group only sees it in the morning.

options.text: Ask who can finish it tonight, and offer to help
options.then: A teammate takes it. You review it together by midnight.

options.text: Tell the teacher the project won't be ready on time
options.then: The teacher asks for an update and marks it as late.

options.text: Wait and hope someone notices the missing part
options.then: Nobody says anything, and the gap is still there at midnight.

steps.why: Naming the gap and sharing the load gets it done without one person burning out.

scenarios.debrief: Taking initiative when there's a gap is exactly what everyday leadership looks like.
scenarios.relearn: Take initiative when there's a gap; that's leadership.

scenarios.hook: In a planning meeting, your teammate Sara's idea is going unheard.
scenarios.setup: Someone louder has just taken over the room.

steps.prompt: Jay says: "Okay, so we go with my plan. Anyone object?"

options.text: "Sara's idea is strong. Can we come back to it?"
options.then: Jay shrugs. "Sure. Sara, go ahead."

options.text: "Sounds fine to me. Let's go."
options.then: Jay nods and moves to the next item. Sara looks down at her notes.

options.text: "Sara, maybe say it louder next time."
options.then: Sara flushes. "I did say it." The moment passes.

options.text: "I had a similar idea too. Mine was about..."
options.then: Jay nods. "Good, tell us more." Sara's idea stays unmentioned.

steps.why: Naming her idea and asking to return to it lifts Sara without speaking for her.

steps.prompt: Sara says quietly: "Um, it was just a small thing. Maybe it's not that good."

options.text: "It's not small. Walk us through how you'd do it."
options.then: Sara takes a breath and starts. The room goes quiet to listen.

options.text: "You're right. Maybe it needs more work."
options.then: Sara nods and retreats. The idea goes no further.

options.text: "Don't worry. I'll explain it for you."
options.then: You explain it. Sara watches her idea go out in your words.

options.text: "Don't say that. Everyone knows you're smart."
options.then: Sara smiles weakly. "Thanks." She still doesn't explain it.

steps.why: Inviting her to explain in her own words keeps the idea hers.

steps.prompt: After the meeting, Sara says: "I never know how to get people to listen."

options.text: "I'll back you. You can say 'let me finish'."
options.then: Sara laughs softly. "I can try that."

options.text: "You should just speak up more."
options.then: Sara's face falls. "I'm trying."

options.text: "It's the loud ones. Don't bother with them."
options.then: She nods, but looks unsure. "I guess."

options.text: "Send me your ideas first and I'll pitch them."
options.then: "Would you?" she says, relieved. She stays out of the room again.

steps.why: Backing her and giving her a phrase of her own helps her claim the floor.

scenarios.relearn: Lifting others' ideas is a powerful, generous form of leadership.

scenarios.hook: Sort: everyday leadership, or just bossiness?

items.text: Helping the team find a direction
Inviting a quiet member to weigh in
Talking over anyone who pushes back

scenarios.relearn: Finding direction, crediting and inviting input is leadership; controlling and credit-grabbing is just bossiness.

scenarios.hook: You could lead quietly by example, or feel you must be the loudest.

steps.prompt: The outgoing captain says a leader has to be the loudest. What do you do?

options.text: Thank him and lead in your own steady style
options.then: He shrugs. "Your call." You start by asking each person what they'd like to do.

options.text: Try to copy his loud style, even though it isn't you
options.then: You shout at practice. The team goes quiet, and you feel like a fraud.

options.text: Hand the lead over to someone louder than you
options.then: A louder teammate takes over, and you step back from the plan.

options.text: Say you don't think leadership matters for a quiz team
options.then: The team shrugs and drifts with no plan.

steps.why: Leading in your own style is steadier than copying one that isn't yours.

steps.prompt: At practice, two members dominate the answers while three stay silent. What do you do?

options.text: Tell the two to talk less, in front of everyone
options.then: The pair go quiet, and the mood turns awkward.

options.text: Let practice run as it is and see what happens
options.then: The same two answer, and the quiet three drift to their phones.

options.text: Make the two loudest members co-leads of the team
options.then: They take charge, and the quiet three say even less.

options.text: Ask the quieter three to write their answers first
options.then: Three answers arrive, and two are ones the loud pair missed.

steps.why: Giving quieter members a way to contribute lets steady leadership work.

steps.prompt: Before the final, the team is anxious and the captain shouts "Focus!" from the back. What do you do?

options.text: Shout "Focus!" louder to show who's in charge
options.then: The team jumps, and a nervous member freezes up.

options.text: Tell the team to ignore him and stay calm, please
options.then: A few nod, and the captain's face closes.

options.text: Quietly check in with each person, one by one
options.then: Each person tells you one worry. The team relaxes a little.

options.text: Ask him to take over the warm-up instead of you
options.then: He does, and you watch the team from the side.

steps.why: A quiet check-in with each person steadies the team more than volume does.

scenarios.debrief: Leadership comes in many styles. Quiet, steady, by-example leadership is just as real.
scenarios.relearn: Lead in your own style; quiet leadership counts as much as loud.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: lifting others up is one of the most respected forms of leadership. Agree?
scenarios.affirm: Leaders who lift others are the ones people most want to follow; it's true strength.
scenarios.relearn: Lifting others up is one of the most respected forms of leadership.

scenarios.hook: Taking the lead on something risks failing publicly.

steps.prompt: Your club needs someone to lead the open-mic night. What do you do?

options.text: Suggest someone else for the job, to stay safe
options.then: A senior agrees to lead, and asks you to handle the performers.

options.text: Step up and say you'll lead it, risks and all
options.then: The club claps. Your stomach flips, and you open a planning doc.

options.text: Offer to help behind the scenes but not to lead
options.then: Someone else leads, and you are put in charge of the performers.

options.text: Wait and see whether anyone else volunteers first
options.then: Two minutes of silence pass. A senior takes it and asks you to handle the performers.

steps.why: Stepping up, risk included, is how leadership starts.

steps.prompt: Three days before, the main performer drops out, and it lands with you. What do you do?

options.text: Tell the club, ask for ideas, and pick a plan
options.then: Four ideas arrive. You choose a backup act and feel steadier.

options.text: Hide the news and hope that she changes her mind
options.then: She doesn't, and the news breaks on the day.

options.text: Blame the performer for it in the group chat
options.then: The chat turns sour, and two members step back.

options.text: Cut it to a short show, and tell no one
options.then: Guests arrive expecting a full night, and the club is caught off guard.

steps.why: Sharing the problem early, with a plan, keeps trust even when things go wrong.

steps.prompt: On the night, the sound system fails and the crowd waits. What do you do?

options.text: Apologise repeatedly and hide backstage
options.then: The crowd shuffles. The silence gets louder.

options.text: Blame the sound crew loudly, in front of all
options.then: The crew stiffens, and the repair slows.

options.text: Call the night off and send everyone home early
options.then: The crowd leaves, and the performers go unheard.

options.text: Tell the crowd plainly, and start an unplugged act
options.then: Some laugh, and the first act goes on acoustic. The crowd settles.

steps.why: Staying calm and giving the crowd something to watch shows a leader owning a wobble.

steps.prompt: After the event, a few people say it was messy. What do you do?

options.text: Say the mess was the sound crew's fault, not yours
options.then: People nod, but the crew stays away from the next event.

options.text: Say you'll never lead an event like this again
options.then: The club looks uneasy. No one offers to lead next time either.

options.text: Thank them, list what went wrong, and plan fixes
options.then: You write three fixes. Two members volunteer for each.

options.text: Change the subject and move on to the next event
options.then: Nothing is said, and the same mistakes return next time.

steps.why: Owning what went wrong and planning fixes turns a stumble into growth.

scenarios.debrief: Real leadership means accepting the risk of a visible stumble. That's part of the role.
scenarios.relearn: Step up to lead even when it risks public failure.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Isha is unsure about a leadership chance.
scenarios.setup: She has just read the notice for team captain.

steps.prompt: Isha says: "Honestly, I'm not the captain type."

options.text: "You'd be great at this. I'll back you. Go for it."
options.then: Isha smiles, unsure. "You really think so?"

options.text: "If you're not sure, maybe wait till next year."
options.then: Isha nods, relieved and a little sad. The notice stays on the board.

options.text: "Well, you are quieter than the others."
options.then: Isha looks at her shoes. "Yeah. True."

options.text: "Let's ask the coach what they're looking for."
options.then: She shrugs. "I guess." She doesn't sound any more sure.

steps.why: Saying you believe in her and will back her is the lift she needs.

steps.prompt: Isha says: "What if I'm bad at it and everyone sees?"

options.text: "Then you learn in public, like everyone does. I'm here."
options.then: Isha laughs. "Okay. That's a lot less scary."

options.text: "You won't be bad. Stop worrying."
options.then: Isha goes quiet. "You can't know that."

options.text: "Then maybe don't put your name in."
options.then: "Fine," she mutters. She keeps staring at the notice, though.

options.text: "I'll apply too, so you're not alone."
options.then: Isha looks surprised. "But then we'd be against each other."

steps.why: Saying it's fine to learn as you go answers her fear, not brushes it off.

steps.prompt: The next day, Isha says: "I've decided to put my name down. Can you help with what to say?"

options.text: "Yes. Tell me why you want it, and we'll shape it."
options.then: She starts talking, then writes it down. "That's actually it."

options.text: "Just copy what the last captain wrote."
options.then: Isha nods, but the words don't sound like her.

options.text: "I'll write it. You just read it out."
options.then: She agrees, relieved. The speech is yours, not hers.

options.text: "Keep it short. Nobody listens to long speeches."
options.then: Isha shrugs. "Okay." She still has nothing written.

steps.why: Helping her find her own words supports her without taking over.

scenarios.hook: Meena raised an idea earlier, and now someone louder is being credited for it.
scenarios.setup: The room is nodding along.

steps.prompt: The lead says: "Brilliant idea, Vikram. That's exactly what we needed."

options.text: "To credit it fairly, it was Meena's idea."
options.then: The lead turns. "Oh. Thanks, Meena." Vikram nods, a little red.

options.text: "Yes, it's a good one."
options.then: The lead nods. Meena looks down and Vikram smiles.

options.text: "Vikram, didn't Meena say that first?"
options.then: Vikram bristles. "I built on it." The room tenses.

options.text: "Great. Let's move on to the budget, then."
options.then: The room moves on. Vikram is still the one credited.

steps.why: Kindly re-crediting in the moment fixes the record where everyone hears it.

steps.prompt: Over lunch, Vikram says: "Meena said something like it first, but I took it further, right?"

options.text: "You did. Just name where it began."
options.then: Vikram pauses. "Fair. I'll say so next time."

options.text: "Further? You took the credit for it."
options.then: Vikram goes cold. The next meeting is tense.

options.text: "Right. It's basically yours now."
options.then: Vikram relaxes. The same thing happens a month later.

options.text: "Did you do it on purpose, though?"
options.then: Vikram flushes. "What? No."

steps.why: Acknowledging his part and asking him to name the origin stays kind and clear.

steps.prompt: Meena asks you: "Next time, how do I cut in and say it was mine?"

options.text: "Try: 'Thanks. That was my idea. Here's the next step.'"
options.then: Meena laughs. "That one I can do."

options.text: "Just speak louder."
options.then: Meena's shoulders drop.

options.text: "Leave it. Credit sorts itself out."
options.then: Meena nods, unconvinced.

options.text: "I'll speak up for you every time."
options.then: Meena smiles, but she stays at the edge of the room.

steps.why: Giving her a line to use herself builds her own voice.

steps.prompt: The lead asks: "Any other ideas?" Meena hesitates and glances at Vikram.

options.text: "Meena, you were about to say something."
options.then: Meena takes a breath and starts. Vikram listens.

options.text: "Vikram, go ahead."
options.then: Vikram speaks. Meena sinks back.

options.text: "Let's move on, then."
options.then: The meeting moves on. Meena's idea stays unspoken.

options.text: "I'll share Meena's idea for her."
options.then: You explain it. Meena watches it leave her hands.

steps.why: Opening the door and letting her speak keeps the idea hers.

scenarios.hook: You catch yourself about to call a woman colleague "bossy" for being assertive.

steps.prompt: Leela firmly asks the team to pick a date and you feel the word coming. What do you do?

options.text: Ask yourself if you'd say it of a man
options.then: You'd have called it decisive from a man. The irritation eases.

options.text: Say it anyway. It's only a word
options.then: Someone laughs. Leela's face stays blank.

options.text: Bite your tongue but stay irritated all day
options.then: The word stays unsaid. The irritation leaks into how you answer her.

options.text: Say it as a joke so it sounds light
options.then: A few people laugh. Leela's smile doesn't reach her eyes.

steps.why: Checking the word against how you'd see a man is how you catch the double standard.

steps.prompt: Later, a friend grumbles that Leela is "so bossy". What do you say?

options.text: Would we call a man that for setting a date?
options.then: Your friend pauses. "Hm. Probably not."

options.text: Ha, yes, she really is like that, isn't she
options.then: Your friend grins. The label spreads through the group.

options.text: Shh. Don't say that where she can hear
options.then: Your friend rolls their eyes. The label stays, just quieter.

options.text: Well, she could soften it a bit
options.then: Your friend nods. "Exactly." Her standard is now stricter than anyone's.

steps.why: Asking how you'd see a man invites your friend to check the label too.

options.then: Leela takes notes. "That's useful. Nobody's been this clear."

options.text: Say she's perfect as she is

options.text: Suggest she tone down her directness
options.then: Leela nods tightly. She starts hedging her asks.

options.text: Mention that some people find her bossy
options.then: Leela's face falls. "Who? What did they mean?" You can't say.

steps.why: Specific feedback, the kind you'd give anyone, helps her without the label.

options.then: The form reads like the ones you'd write for anyone. Leela's review is fair.

options.text: Strong, though maybe she could be a little warmer

options.text: Leave the box blank to avoid the whole issue
options.then: Her leadership goes unrecorded in the review.

steps.why: Describing her by what she did, as for anyone, removes the double standard.

options.text: "Ask Anjali. It's not really my business."

scenarios.hook: A colleague, Sunita, is being harassed at work and isn't sure it counts.

steps.prompt: She tells you a senior keeps commenting on her body. What do you say?

options.text: "I believe you. It counts, and it's not your fault."
options.then: Sunita's shoulders loosen. "I thought I was overreacting."

options.text: "Maybe he's just being friendly."
options.then: Sunita goes quiet. "Maybe. I don't know."

options.text: "That's awful. Report him right now."
options.then: Sunita tenses. "I'm not ready for that."

options.text: "I'll take it to HR for you."
options.then: Sunita looks alarmed. "Please don't. Not without asking me."

steps.why: Believing her and saying it isn't her fault is where support starts.

steps.prompt: Sunita asks whether this is something she can report. What do you say?

options.text: "Yes. The Internal Committee handles this."
options.then: Sunita's eyes widen. "I didn't know it was a real thing."

options.text: "Only if it's physical. Words don't count."
options.then: Sunita's face falls. "So mine doesn't count."

options.text: "You could, but most people just put up with it."
options.then: Sunita nods slowly. "That's what I thought."

options.text: "Ask the HR head to sort it out quietly."
options.then: Sunita looks unsure. "Quietly how?"

steps.why: Harassment has real redress through the Internal Committee. It is never the price of a job.

steps.prompt: Sunita says she's afraid of how he'll react if she reports. What do you say?

options.text: "That makes sense. You set the pace. I'll help."
options.then: Sunita breathes out. "Thank you. I don't have to decide today."

options.text: "Don't wait. It only gets worse if you do."
options.then: Sunita tenses. She feels rushed.

options.text: "Let's go to the committee together right now."
options.then: Sunita freezes. "Right now? I'm not ready."

options.text: "He probably doesn't realise. Talk to him first."
options.then: Sunita shakes her head. "Not alone with him."

steps.why: Respecting her pace, and staying alongside her, keeps the choice hers.

steps.prompt: A week later, Sunita asks who she can call at night if it feels like too much. What do you say?

options.text: "Women Helpline 181 is open any hour. I'm here too."
options.then: Sunita saves the number. "Thanks. That helps."

options.text: "You'll be fine. Try not to think about it."
options.then: Sunita goes quiet and stops asking.

options.text: "Post about it online so others know."
options.then: Sunita looks alarmed. "That could make it worse."

options.text: "I can't help. It's a work matter."
options.then: Sunita nods and withdraws.

steps.why: A trusted person and a helpline she can reach at any hour mean she isn't alone.

options.text: "I've led the survey. I'd like to discuss my role."
options.then: She sits back. "Okay. Tell me what you have in mind."

options.text: "A big raise now, or I'll look elsewhere."
options.then: She stiffens. "That sounds like an ultimatum."

options.text: "Whatever you think is fair, ma'am."
options.then: She shrugs. "Well, let's see what I can do." Nothing concrete is noted.

options.text: "Just a thank-you would be enough."

steps.prompt: She checks the time and says: "I have to run. Can we pick this up later?"

options.text: "Do you need more time? I thought this was simple."
