steps.prompt: The budget turns out tighter than expected, and it's on your desk. What do you do?

options.text: Quietly cut things and hope nobody notices
options.then: A performer notices the missing item and asks why.

options.text: Decide it's too hard and hand the job back
options.then: He takes it back, more surprised than upset.

options.text: Ask the team to cover the gap from their pockets
options.then: A few pay. Others quietly resent it.

options.text: Tell the senior early and suggest two options
options.then: He shows you how to trim. You choose the simpler option.

steps.why: Flagging a problem early, with options, is what trusted leaders do.

scenarios.debrief: Stretch leadership roles grow you. You rarely feel fully ready, and that's normal.
scenarios.relearn: Say yes to stretch leadership roles; you grow into them.

scenarios.hook: A mate teases you about feminism at the tea stall.
scenarios.setup: You've just finished a game of cricket.

steps.prompt: Vikram grins: "Feminism is just anti-men. Admit it."

options.text: "It's about fairness for everyone. Men included."
options.then: He raises an eyebrow. "Men included? Since when?"

options.text: "Yeah, some of it goes too far."
options.then: He nods, pleased, and the joke gets bigger.

options.text: "You don't know anything about it, mate."
options.then: He bristles. "Oh, here we go."

options.text: "Let's not talk politics over chai at the tea stall."
options.then: He laughs, and the claim hangs in the air.

steps.why: A warm, short reframe says equality is on everyone's side.

steps.prompt: The next day Vikram asks: "So what's in it for guys, really?"

options.text: "Nothing for us, but it's the right thing to do."
options.then: He smirks. "Thanks for proving my point."

options.text: "Why does there have to be something in it for you?"
options.then: He shrugs. "Because there is for everyone." The question hangs.

options.text: "Go and read a book about it, yaar."
options.then: He rolls his eyes. "Yeah, no."

options.text: "Less pressure to earn alone. Freedom to ask for help."
options.then: He pauses. "My dad has never asked anyone for help. Ever."

steps.why: Naming real gains for men, like freedom from rigid roles, answers 'what's in it for us'.

steps.prompt: A week on, Vikram jokes to the group: "Watch out, he's turned into a feminist."

options.text: "At least I'm not scared of it, unlike some."
options.then: The laughter stops. Vikram says, "Scared? Of what?"

options.text: "Okay, okay, I'll stop talking about it. Sorry, guys."
options.then: They nod, and the talk slides back to cricket.

options.text: "If fairness is feminism, sure. Who's up for chai?"
options.then: The group laughs, and Vikram hands you a cup.

options.text: "Stop mocking me or I'm leaving."
options.then: A mate says, "Relax, man." Two of them drift away.

steps.why: Answering with humour and warmth keeps the friendship and your view.

scenarios.relearn: Reframe equality as fairness for everyone, men included, not anti-men.

scenarios.hook: Sort: helps you be heard, or fades you out?

items.text: Waiting until the very end, unheard
Building on others, then adding yours
Mumbling so no one's put out

scenarios.relearn: Speaking early, building on others and leading with your point gets you heard; waiting, pre-apologising and mumbling fades you out.

scenarios.hook: "If she really had the talent, the bias wouldn't hold her back."

myth.un: If she had the talent, bias wouldn't hold her back.
myth.re: Bias holds back talented people all the time; that's exactly why it's worth countering.
myth.why: Talent doesn't cancel structural barriers.

scenarios.relearn: Bias holds back talented people; that's why it's worth countering, not proof of less talent.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: being an ally is a daily practice of small actions, not a badge you wear. Agree?
scenarios.affirm: Allyship lives in small daily actions, not in a label; that's what makes it real.
scenarios.relearn: Allyship is a daily practice of small actions, not a badge.

scenarios.hook: Match the leadership move to its effect on a team.
scenarios.relearn: Inviting quieter people in and crediting openly grows a fair team; domination shrinks it.

scenarios.hook: "Taking up space confidently isn't 'ladylike'."

myth.un: Taking up space confidently isn't 'ladylike'.
myth.re: Everyone, of any gender, is entitled to take up space and be heard.
myth.why: 'Ladylike' shouldn't mean small or silent.

scenarios.relearn: Everyone is entitled to take up space and be heard, regardless of gender.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: the generation that makes equality normal at work and home changes everything after. Be part of it?
scenarios.affirm: Normalising equality at work and home is how your generation changes the ones that follow.
scenarios.relearn: Making equality normal at work and home changes everything after.

scenarios.hook: At work, colleagues are chatting about a woman who's just been made team lead.
scenarios.setup: You're all standing by the tea counter.

steps.prompt: A colleague says: "Well, she's just too emotional to lead, isn't she?"

options.text: "Hey, that's not fair. Can we keep it respectful?"
options.then: He pauses. "Okay, okay. I was only saying."

options.text: "Ha. Let's talk about something else, yaar."
options.then: He smirks. "Fine. But you know I'm right."

options.text: "Hm, maybe. I wouldn't really know much about her."
options.then: He takes that as agreement. "Right? Exactly."

options.text: "That's pretty sexist, you know, honestly."
options.then: He rolls his eyes. "Everything is sexist with you people."

steps.why: A calm line names the problem without starting a fight.

steps.prompt: The next day, another colleague says: "Women leaders are always so strict, no?"

options.text: "Stop saying that. It's really offensive, okay?"
options.then: She flushes. "I was only making conversation."

options.text: "I've no view on it. Not my department."
options.then: She shrugs and carries on with her lunch.

options.text: "Strict, or held to a tougher standard than men?"
options.then: She stops. "Hm. Maybe that's it. Nobody calls the men strict."

options.text: "Ha, some of them are, sure enough."
options.then: She nods. The remark goes unchallenged again.

steps.why: A light question shows the double standard without a lecture.

steps.prompt: A newer colleague says quietly: "I never know what to say when someone says that. Do you?"

options.text: "Try: 'That's not really fair.' It gets easier."
options.then: She nods. "Short. I can do short."

options.text: "Just ignore it. It isn't worth the trouble."
options.then: She sighs. She files it away and stays quiet.

options.text: "You'll grow a thicker skin in time, trust me."
options.then: She smiles weakly. Skin was never the problem.

options.text: "Tell the manager about every remark you hear."
options.then: She looks alarmed. "Every single one? That sounds exhausting."

steps.why: A simple, calm call-in line is enough, and it gets easier.

scenarios.relearn: A simple, calm call-in line is enough to interrupt everyday sexism.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a reliable way to build real equality, or just optics?

items.text: Changing how credit and tasks are shared
Talking equality but acting the same
Tracking who gets the visible work

scenarios.relearn: Sharing credit and tasks, mentoring and tracking visible work are real change; slogans, posters and unchanged behaviour are optics.

scenarios.hook: You lead a team and want every member's ideas to shape the plan.

steps.prompt: In the team huddle, the same three people answer everything. What do you do?

options.text: Ask quieter members directly for their thoughts
options.then: Nisha offers a point nobody had considered. The huddle shifts.

options.text: Go with whoever speaks up first, to save time
options.then: The huddle ends in five minutes, and three people sit silent.

options.text: Tell the loudest three to speak less in huddles
options.then: They nod, offended, and the room loses its energy.

options.text: Ask everyone to send ideas by email after the huddle
options.then: A few replies trickle in. The same three dominate the next huddle.

steps.why: Asking quieter people directly draws out voices that a general question misses.

steps.prompt: A quiet member says he doesn't have much to add. What do you do?

options.text: Accept that and move on to the loud ones again
options.then: The huddle speeds on. He stays quiet for the rest.

options.text: Say that everyone must speak, with no excuses
options.then: He speaks, stiffly, and looks away.

options.text: Ask a louder member what he'd probably think
options.then: She guesses. He nods without a word, and his own view stays unheard.

options.text: Say you'd value even a half-formed thought
options.then: He hesitates, then shares an idea that changes the plan.

steps.why: Inviting even a half-formed thought lowers the cost of speaking.

steps.prompt: A week later, a confident member says going round everyone will slow huddles down. What do you say?

options.text: Agree and keep huddles to whoever speaks first
options.then: Huddles stay short, and the quieter members stay silent.

options.text: Tell her that she'll just have to wait her turn
options.then: She folds her arms, and the next huddle is tense.

options.text: Say a few extra minutes bring better ideas for all
options.then: She grumbles, then says she'll give it a try.

options.text: Suggest she skips huddles if she finds them slow
options.then: She shrugs. The team loses her ideas too.

steps.why: Explaining the gain keeps everyone on board while the room stays fair.

scenarios.debrief: Inclusive leaders actively draw out the quieter voices, not just the loud ones.
scenarios.relearn: As a leader, deliberately invite the quieter voices in.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: equal and confident, your voice, your leadership, your allyship, carry all three forward?
scenarios.affirm: Carry your voice, leadership, bias-radar and allyship, and you make every room you enter fairer.
scenarios.relearn: Carry your voice, your leadership, your bias-radar and your allyship forward.

scenarios.hook: "Being an ally means I should speak FOR women, not let them speak."

myth.un: A good ally speaks for women instead of letting them speak.
myth.re: A good ally makes space so they're heard, then steps back; you pass the mic, you don't take it.
myth.why: Allyship amplifies the person, it doesn't replace their voice.

scenarios.relearn: Allyship passes the mic and makes space; it doesn't speak over the people you're backing.

scenarios.hook: "If I'm not the target, it's not my problem to raise."

myth.un: If the bias isn't aimed at me, it's not mine to raise.
myth.re: Allies with no stake in it often carry less risk speaking up, so your voice can land where hers can't.
myth.why: Not being the target is exactly why your backing helps.

scenarios.relearn: Not being the target is why your voice can land safely; speak up anyway.

scenarios.hook: "Allyship is a women's-day post and a panel once a year."

myth.un: Allyship is a women's-day post and one yearly panel.
myth.re: Allyship is what you do on the ordinary days nobody's watching: in the meeting, the chat, the hiring call.
myth.why: The unwatched moments are where allyship is real.

scenarios.relearn: Real allyship is the ordinary unwatched days, not the once-a-year post.

scenarios.hook: "If she didn't ask me to step in, I shouldn't."

myth.un: If she didn't ask me to step in, I shouldn't.
myth.re: You can back her in the moment and check in after; just ask quietly what kind of support she'd want next time.
myth.why: Reading the room plus a quiet check-in beats freezing.

scenarios.relearn: Back her in the moment, then quietly ask what support she'd want next time.

scenarios.hook: "Once I've apologised for a slip-up, the ally work is done."

myth.un: Once I've apologised for a slip, my ally work is done.
myth.re: An apology is step one; allies change the behaviour next time, not just say sorry for this time.
myth.why: Saying sorry without changing anything teaches nothing.

scenarios.relearn: An apology is only step one; allyship changes the behaviour, not just words.

scenarios.hook: "Calling something out always means a big public scene."

myth.un: Calling bias out always means a loud public scene.
myth.re: A quiet word after the meeting, or a private message, often changes more and costs the person less face.
myth.why: Calling in privately gives a real chance to change.

scenarios.relearn: You can call bias in quietly and privately; it isn't always a public scene.

scenarios.hook: In your WhatsApp group, someone forwards a "women drivers" meme and the laughing emojis pile up.
scenarios.setup: Your thumb hovers over the keyboard.

steps.prompt: Kabir, who posted it, writes: "Haha, true or not? Reply, bro."

options.text: "This meme is sexist. Delete it, Kabir, right now."
options.then: Kabir replies, "Chill. It's a joke." Two others go quiet.

options.text: "Ha. Anyway, who's coming on Saturday, everyone?"
options.then: A few people answer about Saturday. The meme sits unanswered.

options.text: "😂😂 Classic one, bro. Send more of those."
options.then: The emojis pile up. The meme stays at the top of the chat.

options.text: "Eh, we can do better than tired ones, na. Skip it."
options.then: Kabir sends a shrug emoji. "Okay, fair. Next one's better."

steps.why: A light nudge breaks the pile-on without a lecture.

steps.prompt: Sana messages you privately: "That meme really got to me. I never know what to say in that group."

options.text: "Let's start a new group without them all."
options.then: Sana hesitates. "That feels like a lot. Can't we just talk?"

options.text: "Probably just the usual. Don't stress about it, okay?"
options.then: Sana types, deletes, and sends a thumbs up.

options.text: "It's just memes. Mute the group for a bit."
options.then: Sana goes quiet. She feels even more alone with it.

options.text: "It got to me too. Say it together next time?"
options.then: Sana sends a heart. "Yes. It's easier if it's not just me."

steps.why: Backing each other makes it easier to speak up next time.

steps.prompt: Kabir posts a meme about wives and cooking and writes: "Only fun, na. Nobody get serious."

options.text: "That's it. I'm leaving this group right now."
options.then: You leave. The jokes carry on with one less voice.

options.text: "😂 Okay, this one is actually funny, bro."
options.then: Kabir sends a fist bump. The pile-on is back.

options.text: "Kabir, you clearly have no respect for women."
options.then: Kabir snaps, "Who asked you?" and the chat turns sour.

options.text: "Not serious, bro. Just not funny to me."
options.then: Kabir pauses. "Okay. Point taken, I guess."

steps.why: A steady, light line keeps the tone without turning it into a fight.

scenarios.relearn: A light, no-lecture nudge in a group chat is enough to break a sexist-meme pile-on.

scenarios.hook: At the team lunch, two men start rating a new female intern's looks.
scenarios.setup: She has just gone to fetch some water.

steps.prompt: One grins: "Out of ten, I'd say eight. What about you?"

options.text: "Let's not rate colleagues. She's here to work."
options.then: He raises his hands. "Okay, okay. Only joking."

options.text: "Ha. Can we talk about something else?"
options.then: The talk shifts, and nobody is told why.

options.text: "That's disgusting. You should both be ashamed."
options.then: They go quiet, then murmur. The lunch turns awkward.

options.text: "Nine, but keep your voice down, yaar."
options.then: They laugh. The rating carries on, just quieter.

steps.why: Naming it plainly stops colleagues being rated on looks.

steps.prompt: The intern returns and asks: "Everything okay? It went quiet."

options.text: "Ask them. I'm staying out of it."
options.then: She looks at the two men, then down at her plate.

options.text: "Nothing worth repeating. How's your week going?"
options.then: She relaxes. "Busy, but good. Thanks for asking."

options.text: "They were rating your looks. Ask them about it."
options.then: She freezes. The lunch is now about her.

options.text: "Nothing at all. It's all fine, really."
options.then: She nods, unsure. She feels the silence was about her.

steps.why: Including her warmly protects her without spotlighting her.

steps.prompt: Later, one of the two says: "Come on. It was harmless, right?"

options.text: "She's a colleague. Please stop rating people."
options.then: He shrugs. "Fine. I didn't think anyone cared."

options.text: "I'll report you both to the manager today."
options.then: He stiffens. "Wow. Over a joke?" He stops talking to you.

options.text: "Maybe. I didn't really mind it myself."
options.then: He nods. "Exactly." Nothing has changed.

options.text: "Harmless, sure. Just keep it quiet next time."
options.then: He grins. "Deal." The habit just moves out of earshot.

steps.why: A plain word in private gives him the chance to change.

scenarios.relearn: Naming it plainly stops colleagues being rated on looks; silence lets it continue.

scenarios.hook: You're on a hiring panel call, and a strong woman candidate is up for discussion.
scenarios.setup: The panel is ready to rank the candidates.

steps.prompt: A panellist says: "She's strong, but she might leave after marriage."

options.text: "True. It's a risk. Let's check others too."
options.then: The panel nods. Her score drops half a point.

options.text: "We don't ask men that. Judge her on the work."
options.then: He shifts. "Fair. I suppose we don't ask men that."

options.text: "That's discrimination. I'm reporting this panel."
options.then: He bristles. "I was only being realistic." The room tenses.

options.text: "Noted. Let's keep moving through the list."
options.then: "Noted," he says. Nobody mentions it again, and it stays beside her name.

steps.why: Applying the same standard to everyone is what makes it fair.

steps.prompt: The chair says: "Let's rank on past projects and interview answers. Any objections?"

options.text: "I'd rank by gut feel for who fits the team."
options.then: The chair pauses. "Gut feel can be slippery."

options.text: "Only if we also count who is likely to stay."
options.then: The chair frowns. "That's a guess, not a score."

options.text: "None. Shall we score all on the same criteria?"
options.then: The chair nods. "Good. A single sheet for everyone."

options.text: "None. I'll go with whatever the panel decides."
options.then: The chair moves on, and the criteria stay loose.

steps.why: A shared scoring sheet makes every candidate count equally.

steps.prompt: After the call, a panellist says: "Fine, but aren't women more likely to leave?"

options.text: "Probably. Maybe ask her about it in round two."
options.then: He nods. The question goes to her and not to the men.

options.text: "Not really. But let's not get into it now."
options.then: He shrugs. The belief is still in the room.

options.text: "You clearly don't respect women at all."
options.then: He snaps. "That's unfair." The talk is over.

options.text: "Anyone can leave. Judge everyone the same way."
options.then: He thinks. "Okay. I'll score her on the work then."

steps.why: "Might leave" is a guess about her, never a fair test.

scenarios.relearn: Apply the same standard to all candidates; 'might leave after marriage' is bias, not a fair test.

scenarios.hook: A senior keeps calling your manager Priya "beta" in front of the team.
scenarios.setup: He does it again as the meeting opens.

steps.prompt: The senior says: "Beta Priya, let me explain how this project works."

options.text: "Yes sir, please explain. We're happy to learn."
options.then: He talks for ten minutes. Priya sits with a fixed smile.

options.text: "Sir, that is very disrespectful of you."
options.then: He goes red. "Who are you to lecture me?" The meeting stalls.

options.text: "It's Priya ma'am, sir. She's leading this one."
options.then: The senior blinks. "Oh. Yes, of course. Priya, go ahead."

options.text: "Priya, shall I tell him this is your project?"
options.then: Priya's smile tightens. "I can speak for myself, thanks."

steps.why: A light correction restores her standing without a confrontation.

steps.prompt: After the meeting, Priya says to you: "He does that all the time. What would you do?"

options.text: "Maybe just smile back. It isn't worth it."
options.then: She sighs. The smile hides how tired she is.

options.text: "I'd have a calm word with him. I can join you."
options.then: Priya exhales. "Okay. A calm word. I'll think about when."

options.text: "I'd complain to the director straight away today."
options.then: She winces. "That's too big a step for now."

options.text: "Honestly? I'd ignore him. He's old-school."
options.then: She nods. "Yes. Everyone says so."

steps.why: A calm word, with support, gives him a chance to change.

steps.prompt: Weeks later, the senior introduces Priya to a client: "This is my junior, Priya."

options.text: "Priya's our project lead. She'll walk you through it."
options.then: The client turns to Priya. "Wonderful. Please begin."

options.text: "Let it go. A client meeting isn't the place."
options.then: The meeting goes on. The client thinks Priya is junior.

options.text: "Junior, yes, but doing great work, sir."
options.then: The client smiles politely. Priya's title stays unclear.

options.text: "Sir, that's wrong. Apologise in front of the client."
options.then: The senior stiffens. The client looks at the table.

steps.why: Naming her role plainly keeps her standing clear.

scenarios.relearn: A light correction restores a colleague's standing when she's talked down to.

scenarios.hook: You're a guest at your sister's in-laws' home, where only she serves tea.
scenarios.setup: Her mother-in-law glances at the tea tray.

steps.prompt: Her mother-in-law tells your sister: "Beta, go and make tea for everyone."

options.text: "Didi, sit. I'll bring the tea round."
options.then: Her mother-in-law hesitates, then nods. "Hm. All right, beta."

options.text: "Why is it always her? That's so unfair."
options.then: The room goes silent. Her mother-in-law hardens and Didi looks mortified.

options.text: "Yes, go on, Didi. Tea would be lovely."
options.then: Didi gets up quietly and heads to the kitchen. The men keep talking.

options.text: "Let's just enjoy sitting. No tea is needed."
options.then: Her mother-in-law frowns. "Guests must have tea." Didi still gets up.

steps.why: Picking up the unshared work lets her sit, without a scene.

steps.prompt: Later, her husband's brother says: "Tea is her job in this house. That's how it's always been."

options.text: "Then your whole family is stuck in the past."
options.then: He bristles. "Now you're insulting us."

options.text: "Fair enough. It's your home and your way."
options.then: He nods, satisfied. The pattern stays where it is.

options.text: "Maybe Didi should raise it herself, no?"
options.then: He frowns. "She never has. Why would she?"

options.text: "Everyone drinks the tea. Sharing is easier for all."
options.then: He shrugs. "Hmm. I never really thought of it like that."

steps.why: A simple, fair reason invites him to share the work.

steps.prompt: On the phone, your sister says: "I'm tired of all of it, but I don't want a fight."

options.text: "Then leave them. You don't deserve this at all."
options.then: She sounds shaken. "It's not that bad. Please don't say that."

options.text: "No fight. I'll help next visit, and I'm with you."
options.then: She pauses. "Okay. It helps knowing you're on my side. I'll go at my own pace."

options.text: "Then just bear it. It gets easier with time."
options.then: She says nothing. The tiredness is still there.

options.text: "I'll talk to your in-laws myself next visit."
options.then: She sighs. "Please don't. I'd rather handle it my way."

steps.why: Backing her, at her pace, lightens the load without a fight.

scenarios.relearn: Allyship at home means picking up the unshared work, not waiting to be asked.

scenarios.hook: A trans classmate, Aanya, is being deadnamed by her lab partner.
scenarios.setup: You are at the next bench, in the middle of the lab.

steps.prompt: The lab partner grins: "It's only a joke, yaar. I'm just using her old name."

options.text: "Ha. Just don't do it in front of the teacher."
options.then: He laughs. "Deal." The jokes carry on out of earshot.

options.text: "That's hateful. I'll report you to the professor."
options.then: He glares. "You're overreacting." The bench falls silent.

options.text: "Not my business. She can tell you herself."
options.then: Aanya, at the next bench, pretends not to hear. Nobody backs her.

options.text: "Her name's Aanya. Let's just use it, yeah?"
options.then: He shrugs, a little embarrassed. "Okay. Aanya. Fine."

steps.why: Using her real name plainly backs her, with no lecture.

steps.prompt: Aanya says quietly to you after class: "I'm not sure I want to report it. What do you think?"

options.text: "You should report it today. It's the only real way."
options.then: She frowns. "I don't want to be told what to do."

options.text: "Not your fault. Your call. I'll come with you if you report."
options.then: She nods slowly. "That helps. Let me think, and I'll tell you."

options.text: "Maybe don't. It could make things worse for you."
options.then: She nods, but she looks even more uncertain.

options.text: "I'll report it for you. You won't have to face them."
options.then: She hesitates. "Please don't. I want to decide myself."

steps.why: It's never her fault. Her call, with an offer to go with her, keeps her in charge.

steps.prompt: In the next lab, another classmate asks: "Why is everyone using a new name for her?"

options.text: "It's a long story. Don't get into it."
options.then: The classmate looks curious. The whispers go on.

options.text: "Because it's her name. Simple as that."
options.then: The classmate nods. "Okay. Got it."

options.text: "She's going through something. Be kind about it."
options.then: The classmate nods gravely. Aanya now sounds like a problem.

options.text: "Ask her yourself. I'm not the one to explain."
options.then: The classmate shrugs. Nobody explains it to them.

steps.why: Using her name, with no fuss, makes it normal.

scenarios.relearn: Using someone's real name and correcting a deadname is concrete, inclusive allyship.

scenarios.hook: Arjun built the team's slide deck almost alone, and today it's being reviewed.
scenarios.setup: Your manager flicks through the slides, smiling.

steps.prompt: Your manager says: "Thanks, girls, for making the deck so pretty."

options.text: "'Girls'? That's sexist. Apologise to everyone, sir."
options.then: The manager stiffens. "I meant it kindly." The room cools.

options.text: "Glad you like it, sir. Happy to help."
options.then: The manager beams. Arjun looks down at the table.

options.text: "Arjun, say something. It's your work, after all."
options.then: Arjun mumbles, "It's fine." The moment passes.

options.text: "Actually, Arjun built that deck. Full credit to him."
options.then: The manager turns. "Arjun? I didn't realise. Thanks, Arjun."

steps.why: Naming who did the work is fair to everyone involved.

steps.prompt: Arjun says later: "I didn't know what to say in there. Was that 'girls' comment a bit off?"

options.text: "I'll sort it out with the manager on my own."
options.then: He looks relieved. He also learns nothing about what to say.

options.text: "You should have spoken up. It was your work."
options.then: He looks down. "I know. Now I feel worse."

options.text: "Yes. Next time let's speak up together."
options.then: He nods. "Okay. I'd rather we did it together."

options.text: "Not really. Forget it. It's over now."
options.then: He shrugs. Nothing changes for next time.

steps.why: Speaking up together makes it easier for everyone.

steps.prompt: A month on, your manager asks: "Who should lead the next deck?"

options.text: "Arjun, since he's fast. Let him do them all."
options.then: Arjun gets every deck from now on. Nobody else learns, and he's stretched thin.

options.text: "Let's rotate the lead and credit each part."
options.then: The manager nods. "A rotation. Fine. Send me the plan."

options.text: "Whoever's free. It doesn't really matter."
options.then: The manager picks whoever is nearest. Credit gets fuzzy again.

options.text: "Me. The others can help with the design."
options.then: The manager nods. Your name tops the deck, and the others get the "pretty" part again.

steps.why: Rotating the work, and naming each part, makes credit fair.

scenarios.relearn: Correcting mis-credited work, even across gender lines, is even-handed allyship.

scenarios.hook: On the late shift, your colleague Neha's auto hasn't come, and the area feels unsafe.
scenarios.setup: Everyone else has already left for the night.

steps.prompt: Neha says: "My ride is late. You can go. I'll manage."

options.text: "Okay. Text me when you're home safe."
options.then: You leave. Ten minutes later, Neha calls you: her ride still hasn't come.

options.text: "I'll wait with you till your ride's here, no rush."
options.then: Neha smiles with relief. "Thanks. I wasn't looking forward to standing here alone."

options.text: "Are you sure? I have a long commute myself."
options.then: Neha shrugs. "It's fine. Go." She glances at the empty lane.

options.text: "Just take any auto you find on the main road."
options.then: Neha looks uneasy. A stranger's auto at this hour isn't what she wanted.

steps.why: Waiting with her is small, practical support she didn't have to ask for.

steps.prompt: Her ride app shows a twenty-minute wait. Neha asks: "Should I just walk to the main road?"

options.text: "Wait at the office till morning. It's not worth the risk."
options.then: She nods, but the thought of a night at the office makes her tired.

options.text: "Yes, go ahead. Main roads are always fine."
options.then: She sets off alone down the dark lane. You wonder if you should have said more.

options.text: "Let's book a cab. Send the trip to someone you trust."
options.then: Neha shares her live trip with her sister. "Okay. That feels safer."

options.text: "It's only ten minutes. You'll be perfectly fine."
options.then: Neha's shoulders tense. She has already imagined the ten minutes.

steps.why: A booked cab, with trip details shared with someone she trusts, lowers the risk.

steps.prompt: Next week, Neha asks: "Late shifts make me nervous. Should I tell the manager?"

options.text: "Then just avoid the late shifts from now on."
options.then: She nods. But she's now the one who misses late shifts.

options.text: "Yes. I'll back you, and we can ask for cab support."
options.then: Neha nods. "Okay. I'd feel better if it wasn't only me asking."

options.text: "I'll tell the manager for you. Don't worry."
options.then: She looks uneasy. "I'd rather say it myself, with you there."

options.text: "Better not. It might look like you can't cope."
options.then: Neha's face falls. She says nothing more about it.

steps.why: Feeling unsafe is never her fault. Asking for safer late-shift support is reasonable.

scenarios.relearn: Waiting with a colleague until her ride comes is small, practical allyship.

scenarios.hook: Your teammate Vikram brags that he never lets his wife work, and others nod along.
scenarios.setup: He says it at the tea break.

steps.prompt: Vikram laughs: "A wife's place is at home. Ask anyone here."

options.text: "If she wants to work, why hold her back? Her call, na."
options.then: Vikram frowns. "Hmm. She's never actually asked, to be honest."

options.text: "Let's not talk about other people's wives, yaar."
options.then: A few others mutter agreement. The remark stands unchallenged.

options.text: "Haha, each to their own, bro."
options.then: Vikram grins. The others nod, and the topic stays where it was.

options.text: "That's so backward. You're controlling her, honestly."
options.then: Vikram snaps. "Mind your own house." The group goes stiff.

steps.why: Whether she works is her call. A calm question opens it up.

steps.prompt: Another teammate says: "Vikram's right. Family honour matters, yaar."

options.text: "You may have a point there, to be fair."
options.then: He looks pleased. The nodding starts up again.

options.text: "Some families do it differently, and that's fine."
options.then: He nods. The idea of permission sits unchallenged.

options.text: "Honour? That's just an excuse for control, honestly."
options.then: He reddens. "You're judging my family now."

options.text: "Honour comes from respect, not permission. It's her call."
options.then: He pauses. "That's a different way to see it."

steps.why: Respect, not permission, is what keeps a household fair.

steps.prompt: Later, Vikram says quietly: "My wife wants to study again. Should I let her?"

options.text: "It's not yours to allow. Ask her and back it."
options.then: He thinks. "True. I'll ask her tonight."

options.text: "Maybe, if the family agrees to it all."
options.then: He sighs. Now it's the whole family's permission.

options.text: "Do what's best for the house, bro."
options.then: He nods. She still hasn't been asked.

options.text: "Only if the money works out for you first."
options.then: He nods. The question stays about his budget.

steps.why: It's her decision. The best support is to ask her and back what she wants.

scenarios.relearn: A calm question can challenge a controlling norm without turning it into a fight.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Dev keeps cutting off his girlfriend Tara when you all hang out.

steps.prompt: Tara starts a story and Dev cuts in again. What do you do?

options.text: Say "Tara, go on. I want to hear the end"
options.then: Tara smiles and carries on. Dev shifts in his seat but lets her finish.

options.text: Let it go, since they're a couple
options.then: Tara trails off and sips her chai. Dev finishes her story.

options.text: Tell Dev off in front of everyone
options.then: Dev goes red and snaps back. The evening turns awkward.

options.text: Change the subject so it isn't awkward
options.then: Everyone relaxes. Tara's story is never finished.

steps.why: Handing the floor back in the moment helps without making a scene.

steps.prompt: The next day, Dev calls you about the weekend. His habit of cutting Tara off is on your mind. What do you do?

options.text: Ask Tara to tell Dev to stop it
options.then: Tara says she'd rather not have to. She'd hoped someone else might say it.

options.text: Tell him he cuts Tara off, and ask him to watch it
options.then: He goes quiet, then says: "Okay. I'll watch it."

options.text: Chat about the weekend and leave it alone
options.then: He hangs up cheerful. The pattern carries on unmentioned.

options.text: Tell him Tara deserves far better than someone like him
options.then: He bristles. "That's a bit much. Who are you to say that?"

steps.why: An honest, private word gives him a chance to change.

steps.prompt: At the next hangout, Dev cuts Tara off once more. What do you do?

options.text: Give him a look and say nothing
options.then: Dev doesn't notice the look. Tara's sentence disappears.

options.text: Let it slide, since change takes time
options.then: Change stays slow, and Tara stays quiet for the rest of the evening.

options.text: Say "Let Tara finish, Dev" and smile
options.then: Dev pauses. "Right. Sorry, Tara. Go on."

options.text: Announce to the group that Dev keeps interrupting
options.then: Everyone goes silent. Dev glares at you and Tara looks away.

steps.why: A light, clear nudge in the moment keeps changing the habit.

scenarios.debrief: Redirect in the moment, then have the honest word privately; allyship without a scene.
scenarios.relearn: Redirect to her in the moment and have the honest word with him privately.

scenarios.hook: A junior woman's private photo is posted in a big WhatsApp group you're in.

steps.prompt: Within minutes, people start forwarding it to other chats. What do you do?

options.text: Leave the group without a word
options.then: You're out of it, and the photo keeps circulating without you.

options.text: Delete it from your phone and stay quiet
options.then: Your phone is clean. The photo keeps going round the group.

options.text: Refuse to forward it and say it's not okay
options.then: A few people go quiet. One replies, "Yeah, enough. Delete it."

options.text: Ask in the group who sent it first
options.then: Three people reply with jokes. The photo is still being forwarded.

steps.why: Refusing to pass it on, and saying so, helps stop it spreading.

steps.prompt: The photo is of Nisha, a junior. You want to reach out. What do you do?

options.text: Message her: "A photo of you is going round. Not your fault."
options.then: Nisha reads it twice. "Thank you for telling me. I didn't know who to ask."

options.text: Send her a screenshot so she can see exactly what's going round
options.then: She panics at the sight of it. She might not have wanted to see that.

options.text: Tell her close friends first so they can look after her
options.then: Her friends rush to her. Nisha feels the whole batch now knows.

options.text: Ask her how the photo got out there
options.then: Nisha goes silent. The question makes her feel blamed.

steps.why: Telling her gently, without the image, and saying it isn't her fault lets her choose what's next.

steps.prompt: Later, Nisha is scared and unsure what to do, and turns to you. What do you say?

options.text: "Let me find out who sent it and go deal with them myself."
options.then: Nisha panics. "Please don't. It will only make it worse."

options.text: "Just ignore the group. Nobody remembers these things for long."
options.then: She goes quiet. Pretending it isn't there doesn't make her feel safe.

options.text: "Not your fault. Internal Committee or Women Helpline 181 can help."
options.then: Nisha breathes out. "Okay. Can you come with me once I decide?"

options.text: "Just delete your own copies. It should die down soon enough."
options.then: She nods, but the photo is still out there and she's alone with it.

steps.why: It is never her fault. Support and real routes to help let her choose.

scenarios.debrief: Don't forward it, say it's wrong, and let her know. It is never her fault.
scenarios.relearn: Refuse to forward, say it's not okay, and let the person know.

scenarios.hook: Two seniors want to give a big account to a man because Nandini is expecting.

steps.prompt: You overhear the plan before anyone tells her. What do you do?

options.text: Assume they know best and stay quiet
options.then: The plan goes ahead. Nandini hears about it from a client.

options.text: Tell them she must get the account, no discussion
options.then: They bristle. "Don't tell us how to run things." It becomes an argument.

options.text: Agree it's thoughtful of them to lighten her load
options.then: They smile, pleased. Nobody asks Nandini anything.

options.text: Ask them: "Has anyone asked Nandini what she wants?"
options.then: One senior shifts. "Fair. We assumed. Let's ask her."

steps.why: Asking that she be asked keeps the choice with her.

steps.prompt: Nandini hears of the seniors' plan for the account and asks what you think she should do. What do you say?

options.text: "Let it go. I'm sure nobody meant any harm by it."
options.then: She swallows it. The assumption stays in place for next time.

options.text: "Tell them what you want. I'll back you if you like."
options.then: She nods slowly. "Okay. I'd like the account, with some flexibility."

options.text: "Take the next big one and prove them all wrong."
options.then: She laughs, but it sounds like a burden more than a choice.

options.text: "I'll have it out with them for you."
options.then: She looks uneasy. "I'd rather say it myself, in my own way."

steps.why: Backing her while she speaks for herself keeps the choice hers.

steps.prompt: Later, the seniors ask the team how to share out big accounts in future. What do you suggest?

options.text: Ask each person what they can take on
options.then: The seniors agree to check with everyone, every time.

options.text: Leave it to the manager to guess
options.then: The manager guesses, and the same assumptions come back.

options.text: Go by seniority only, for simplicity
options.then: Big accounts go by rank. Two juniors who wanted one are never asked.

options.text: Give women lighter loads by default, to be kind
options.then: The women on the team get lighter loads. Nobody asks whether they wanted that.

steps.why: Asking people, not assuming for them, is fair to everyone.

scenarios.debrief: Don't let people decide for her; ask that she be asked. The choice is hers.
scenarios.relearn: Surface assumptions made for someone; ask that the person be asked what they want.

scenarios.hook: In your project group, Isha always ends up with the notes and the snack run.

steps.prompt: Today the group turns to her again. What do you do?

options.text: Joke that she's the group's unofficial manager
options.then: Everyone laughs, Isha included. She takes the notes anyway.

options.text: Offer to do the notes just for today
options.then: Isha gets a break today. It's a one-off, and the pattern stays.

options.text: Propose rotating notes and errands every meeting
options.then: The group agrees. A rota goes up on the chat before the meeting ends.

options.text: Leave it, since she's so good at it
options.then: Isha takes the notes and buys the snacks. Nobody notices the pattern.

steps.why: A rota shares the unglamorous work fairly instead of defaulting it to one person.

steps.prompt: Next week, Varun is asked to take the notes. He says he'd only mess them up. What do you say?

options.text: "Isha, you don't mind doing them again, right?"
options.then: Isha shrugs. "Sure." The notes are hers again.

options.text: "Notes are a skill anyone learns. Take this week."
options.then: Varun groans, then opens a fresh page. "Fine. Show me your format."

options.text: "Fair enough. Varun can stick to the slides."
options.then: Varun relaxes. The notes drift back to Isha.

options.text: "Let's leave it to whoever's free each week."
options.then: Isha is always first to open a page. The notes land with her.

steps.why: Everyone can learn the admin tasks, so everyone takes a turn.

steps.prompt: For the final project, your guide asks the group to list who does what. What do you suggest?

options.text: Put Isha on notes and planning, since she's good at it
options.then: Isha nods. The admin is hers again, by default.

options.text: Let each person pick whatever job they like
options.then: The slides and the talk go first. The notes are left for Isha.

options.text: Only list the slides and the talk, since those get marked
options.then: The sheet looks tidy. The notes and planning stay invisible.

options.text: List notes and planning as named roles, and rotate them
options.then: The guide nods. "Good. Every role goes on the sheet."

steps.why: Naming the admin as real roles, and rotating them, means it counts and gets shared.

scenarios.debrief: Office housework is rotated, not defaulted; proposing a rota is everyday allyship.
scenarios.relearn: Propose rotating notes and errands so admin is shared, not defaulted to one person.

scenarios.hook: You lead a small team. Pooja is quiet in standup, and her ideas get skipped.

steps.prompt: Pooja mentions an idea and the talk rolls past her. What do you do?

options.text: Return to it: "Pooja, say more on that."
options.then: The team goes quiet, then asks Pooja two questions. She explains.

options.text: Tell her privately to be more assertive
options.then: Pooja nods, but looks deflated. The problem now sounds like hers.

options.text: Keep standup moving, since time is short
options.then: Standup ends on time. Pooja's idea is lost.

options.text: Wait and see if she repeats it herself
options.then: She waits for a gap that never comes. Standup ends.

steps.why: As the lead, inviting her in by name makes space for her.

steps.prompt: Two days later, Arjun pitches an idea close to Pooja's and the team loves it. What do you do?

options.text: Say "Great idea" and let Arjun take it forward
options.then: Arjun is thanked. Pooja's name never comes up.

options.text: Stay silent so Arjun isn't embarrassed
options.then: Arjun beams. Pooja looks at her notebook.

options.text: Say "That builds on Pooja's idea from Monday"
options.then: Pooja looks up, surprised. Arjun nods. "Right. Pooja, join me on this?"

options.text: Thank Arjun, then tell Pooja privately it was hers
options.then: Pooja smiles thinly. The team still thinks it's Arjun's.

steps.why: Crediting openly grows a fair team.

steps.prompt: You are setting standup habits for the quarter. What do you add?

options.text: Ask quieter people to send ideas in writing
options.then: Some send notes, but the room never hears them.

options.text: Go round everyone by name and credit each idea
options.then: The team tries it. Pooja speaks twice in the first week.

options.text: Keep it as is, since people should speak up more
options.then: Nothing changes, and quiet voices stay quiet.

options.text: Let people speak when they feel ready
options.then: The same three voices fill the time.

steps.why: A shared structure, not pressure on her, is the lead's job.

scenarios.debrief: As the lead, deliberately invite quieter voices and credit them; the room's job, not just hers.
scenarios.relearn: Lead by inviting quieter voices in by name and crediting them openly.

scenarios.hook: A colleague, Imran, comes out to you as gay and asks you to tell no one yet.

steps.prompt: He looks nervous after saying it. What do you do?

options.text: Thank him for trusting you and keep it private
options.then: His shoulders drop. "Thank you. I needed to say it to someone."

options.text: Ask how long he's known and if he's sure
options.then: Imran hesitates. He feels like he's being examined.

options.text: Tell a supportive friend so he has more backing
options.then: Your friend is kind. Imran hadn't agreed to anyone else knowing.

options.text: Say you always suspected it
options.then: Imran winces. "Was I that obvious?"

steps.why: Coming out is his to share. Trust is kept by keeping the confidence.

steps.prompt: At lunch a colleague jokes that Imran never mentions a girlfriend. What do you do?

options.text: Change the topic lightly without saying anything about him
options.then: Lunch moves on to cricket. Imran catches your eye and relaxes.

options.text: Tell the colleague to stop gossiping in front of everyone
options.then: All eyes turn to Imran. He wishes he could disappear.

options.text: Say he's probably just private, with a knowing look
options.then: The look lingers. Two colleagues exchange glances.

options.text: Wink at Imran so he knows you're covering for him
options.then: He sees the wink. So does someone across the table.

steps.why: Changing the subject protects his privacy without drawing attention.

steps.prompt: Imran says he might tell the team one day, but isn't ready. What do you say?

options.text: "The sooner the better. You'll feel lighter."
options.then: He tenses. "Maybe. I just don't want a deadline."

options.text: "It might be easier to keep it hidden at work."
options.then: He looks away. You've made his choice sound like a problem.

options.text: "Want me to tell them for you, to make it easier?"
options.then: He shakes his head. "No. I want to be the one who says it."

options.text: "Whenever you want. I'll follow your lead."
options.then: He nods. "That takes the pressure off. Thank you."

steps.why: Following his lead keeps the decision his.

scenarios.debrief: Coming out is his to control; keep the confidence and follow his lead on support.
scenarios.relearn: Keep a confidence, never out someone, and ask how they want to be supported.

scenarios.hook: You're on a panel where every other speaker is a man, and the organiser says no women applied.

steps.prompt: He says the panel is set and the poster goes out tomorrow. What do you do?

options.text: Suggest names of qualified women and ask to reopen it
options.then: The organiser pauses. "Send me the names. I'll extend the call."

options.text: Mention it on social media after the event
options.then: The post gets likes. The panel has already happened.

options.text: Accept it, since you can't fix the pool
options.then: The poster goes out as planned. Nobody asks about the gap.

options.text: Step down from the panel without suggesting anyone
options.then: You're replaced within a day by another man. The panel looks the same.

steps.why: "None applied" is a reason to widen the search, not a verdict.

steps.prompt: Rhea, a researcher you know, isn't sure she's expert enough for panels. What do you say?

options.text: "You know this work well. I'll introduce you."
options.then: Rhea laughs nervously. "Okay. Tell them I'd be glad to."

options.text: "Do it as a favour, to fix the numbers."
options.then: Rhea frowns. She doesn't want to be the fix.

options.text: "It's fine to skip. They'll find someone."
options.then: She looks relieved, and the panel stays as it is.

options.text: "You're right. Wait until you've published more."
options.then: She nods. "Maybe next year, then."

steps.why: Naming her expertise, and opening the door, matters more than a favour.

steps.prompt: For future panels, the organiser asks how to find good speakers. What do you say?

options.text: Stick with people everyone already knows
options.then: The panel is easy to fill. It's the same panel again.

options.text: Invite exactly one woman per panel as a fixed rule
options.then: The panel gets one woman. The pool stays narrow.

options.text: Wait for volunteers to apply
options.then: The same volunteers apply. The pool looks the same.

options.text: Ask widely, set clear criteria, and keep a list
options.then: The organiser writes it down. "A list. Yes, I'll start one."

steps.why: A wider, fairer search finds people who were already there.

scenarios.debrief: 'No women applied' is a search to widen, not a verdict; offer names and reopen it.
scenarios.relearn: Widen the search and suggest qualified people rather than accepting 'none applied'.

scenarios.hook: Your team jokes that Sameer, who took paternity leave, isn't serious about work.

steps.prompt: Another joke about him lands at the coffee machine. What do you do?

options.text: Laugh along, since it's only harmless banter
options.then: The joke gets a bigger laugh. Sameer, nearby, pretends not to hear.

options.text: Stay quiet and sip your coffee instead
options.then: Nobody notices you didn't laugh. The jokes carry on next week.

options.text: Say: "Looking after a newborn is serious work."
options.then: The laughter stops. Someone mutters, "Fair point, yaar."

options.text: Call them all sexist in front of everyone
options.then: They go defensive. "Relax, it's only a joke." The point gets lost.

steps.why: A calm line backs him up and says that care work counts.

steps.prompt: Sameer says he worried how people would see his leave. What do you say?

options.text: "Ignore what people say. Their problem, not yours."
options.then: He shrugs. It helps less than he hoped.

options.text: "Yes, it does look bad. Just be ready for it."
options.then: Sameer's face falls. He wonders if he made a mistake.

options.text: "Do some check-in calls so they see you're serious."
options.then: He nods slowly. Now he feels he has to prove something.

options.text: "Taking it was fine. I'll keep backing you."
options.then: Sameer smiles. "Good to know someone thinks so."

steps.why: Backing him openly helps more than advice to toughen up.

steps.prompt: A colleague asks whether to take his full paternity leave when the time comes. What do you say?

options.text: "Take it only if you can handle the looks."
options.then: He frowns. The looks now seem bigger than the leave.

options.text: "It's yours to take. Plan the handover and go."
options.then: He grins. "Good. I was hoping someone would say that."

options.text: "Ask the boss first whether it's okay to."
options.then: He hesitates. Leave he's entitled to now needs permission.

options.text: "Take a week. Nobody takes the whole thing."
options.then: He nods, doubtful. The full leave sounds out of reach.

steps.why: Equal roles at home lift everyone, men included.

scenarios.debrief: Backing a man who shares the care load is allyship too; equality frees everyone's roles.
scenarios.relearn: Defend men who share caregiving; equal roles lift everyone, not just women.

scenarios.hook: Your teammate Farah confides that a vendor keeps harassing her, and she's scared to report.

steps.prompt: She is tense and close to tears as she tells you. What do you do?

options.text: March over and confront the vendor yourself
options.then: Farah panics. "Please don't. He'll know I told someone."

options.text: Tell her she has to report it today, no excuses
options.then: Farah stiffens. "I'm not ready. Please don't push me."

options.text: Believe her, say it's not her fault, and listen
options.then: Farah's shoulders drop. "Thank you. I thought no one would believe me."

options.text: Tell her vendors are like that and to ignore him
options.then: Farah nods and stops talking, but the fear stays on her face.

steps.why: Believing her and saying it's not her fault comes first.

steps.prompt: A few days later, Farah quietly asks you what her options are. What do you say?

options.text: "Just avoid the vendor from now on, if you can."
options.then: She agrees, but he is still on her calls every week.

options.text: "Let me handle it quietly with your manager for you."
options.then: She pauses. "I'd rather choose who is told. Please don't."

options.text: "Wait and see whether it stops by itself, maybe."
options.then: Nothing changes that week. The messages keep coming.

options.text: "Try the Internal Committee, or call Women Helpline 181."
options.then: Farah writes it down. "I didn't know that. Would you come with me?"

steps.why: Giving her real routes, and letting her choose, respects her pace.

steps.prompt: Farah says the vendor messaged again and she feels unsafe. What do you do?

options.text: Tell her to block him and try to forget it
options.then: She blocks his number. Told to forget it, she carries the fear alone.

options.text: Message the vendor yourself to tell him to stop
options.then: He replies rudely, and now he knows Farah told someone.

options.text: Help her keep the messages, and offer to go with her
options.then: She sends you screenshots. "Okay. I think I'm ready to tell them."

options.text: Tell your boss everything, without asking her
options.then: Your boss calls Farah in. She feels her choice was taken from her.

steps.why: It is never her fault. Saved proof and a friend by her side keep her choices open.

scenarios.debrief: Believe her, follow her lead, and stand beside her, not in front. It is never her fault.
scenarios.relearn: Believe someone harassed, ask what they want, and offer to go with them.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: drop each into the bin. Real ally move, or just looking like one?

items.text: Crediting a colleague's idea by name
Adding your logo to a women's-day banner
Mentoring a junior through a stretch task

scenarios.relearn: Crediting, mentoring and rotating admin are real ally moves; banners, hashtags and bragging are optics.

Saying 'let her finish' in the moment
Telling yourself it's not your place

scenarios.relearn: Handing the floor back and refusing to forward back people up; waiting and watching is standing by.

"I don't think that's fair on her."

scenarios.relearn: Naming it kindly and a quiet private word call bias in; name-calling and mocking just have a go.

items.text: Confronting her boss without telling her

scenarios.hook: Lensy: sort each. Shares the load fairly, or quietly dumps it?

items.text: Rotating who organises the team party
Always leaving cleanup to the women
Taking minutes turn and turn about
Defaulting snack runs to the juniors
Letting one person carry every errand

scenarios.relearn: Rotating parties, minutes and admin shares the load; defaulting cleanup, snacks and errands to one group dumps it.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: sort each. Includes everyone, or quietly leaves people out?

items.text: Planning every team event at a bar
Asking the new joiner for their take
Inside jokes that freeze out the quiet ones
Talking only to the senior men

scenarios.relearn: Right names, asking newcomers and looping people in includes everyone; senior-only chat leaves people out.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: sort each. A men-as-allies strength, or a tired excuse?

items.text: Sharing the care load at home openly
"It's not a man's place to speak on this"
Backing a woman colleague's idea out loud
"I don't want to overstep" as a dodge

scenarios.relearn: Sharing care, backing colleagues and mentoring is ally strength; 'not my place' and 'not my issue' are excuses.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: in this meeting, spot the two bystander moves that let bias slide.

scene.text: You redirect the question to the woman who was cut off
You credit the junior whose idea got borrowed
You laugh when her point is dismissed as 'emotional'
You stay silent, sure someone else will say it
You ask the quiet teammate for their view

scenarios.why: Laughing along and staying silent are the bystander moves.
scenarios.relearn: Laughing along and staying silent let bias slide; allies back people up out loud.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: in this group chat, tap the two messages that cross a line.

scene.text: "Nice work on the demo, team."
"Forward her photo, it's funny."
"Let's not rate her looks, yeah?"
"She only got it 'cause she's a girl."
"Can someone share the meeting notes?"

scenarios.why: Forwarding her photo and 'only because she's a girl' are the red flags; the rest are fine or are the ally pushing back.
scenarios.relearn: Spreading private photos and crediting bias, not merit, are red flags worth calling out.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: someone calls this 'allyship'. Tap the two moves that are really just optics.

scene.text: Mentors a junior woman through a tough quarter
Posts a long thread about how much he supports women
Rotates note-taking across the team
Adds 'ally' to his bio, changes nothing at work
Credits her idea openly in the review

scenarios.why: The thread and the bio with no change are optics.
scenarios.relearn: Threads and bio tags with no change are optics; mentoring and crediting are real allyship.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: a friend wants to 'help' a harassed colleague. Tap the two moves that overstep her.

scene.text: Asks her what support she'd want
Confronts the harasser without telling her
Offers to go with her if she reports
Posts her story to 'raise awareness'
Keeps what she shared in confidence

scenarios.why: Confronting without asking and posting her story take her choice away.
scenarios.relearn: Confronting or posting without her say overstep; good allies ask and follow her lead.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: at this hostel, spot the two lines that police a man out of caregiving.

scene.text: "Good on you for cooking for your roommates."
"Changing nappies? That's the wife's job, bhai."
"Take the paternity leave, you've earned it."
"Real men don't do the dishes."
"Splitting chores fairly just makes sense."

scenarios.why: 'That's the wife's job' and 'real men don't do dishes' box men out of care.
scenarios.relearn: Lines that box men out of caregiving are red flags; shared roles lift everyone.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: in this hiring call, tap the two comments that are bias dressed as 'practical'.

scene.text: "Score every candidate on the same rubric."
"She'll leave after marriage, skip her."
"His portfolio is the strongest, clearly."
"A woman can't handle late client calls."
"Ask all of them about availability."

scenarios.why: 'Leave after marriage' and 'can't handle late calls' are bias.
scenarios.relearn: 'Practical' guesses about marriage or capability are bias; one fair standard for all isn't.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: a teammate is 'including' a queer colleague. Tap the two moves that exclude.

scene.text: Uses the name and pronoun they asked for
Outs them to the team without asking
Invites them into the discussion
Makes them the butt of a 'harmless' joke
Asks how they'd like to be supported

scenarios.why: Outing them and joking at their expense exclude and harm.
scenarios.relearn: Outing someone or joking at their expense excludes; right names and inviting in include.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: in this standup, spot the two habits that quietly shrink a quieter teammate.

scene.text: The lead asks her by name for her view
Someone talks over her the second she starts
Her idea is credited to whoever said it loudest
The lead circles back to her unfinished point
People wait for her to finish before replying

scenarios.why: Talking over her and re-crediting her idea shrink her.
scenarios.relearn: Talking over someone and re-crediting their idea shrink them; make space instead.

pairs.right: Hand the floor back to her

A sexist joke in the group
A colleague comes out to you

scenarios.relearn: Every everyday moment has a concrete ally move; match the moment to the move.

pairs.right: Gives a real chance to change

scenarios.relearn: Each ally move works for a reason; match the move to why it lands.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: match each ally-fail to the better move beside it.
scenarios.relearn: Every ally-fail has a better move; match the slip to the fix.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: match each line to the kind of move it is.
scenarios.relearn: Each everyday line is a kind of ally move; match the line to the move.
