options.then: She notices it in the submission and says nothing.

options.text: Drop your whole plan and do exactly what she says
options.then: The report loses its thread, and nobody seems to be steering.

steps.why: Testing her idea against yours keeps what works and credits her.

steps.prompt: The reworked report scores higher. The professor asks what changed. What do you say?

options.text: Say it came down to your leadership, mostly
options.then: The professor raises an eyebrow. Two teammates look away.

options.text: Say it was mostly luck and you can't say why
options.then: The professor frowns. The team's effort goes unrecorded.

options.text: Let the teammate who talks most answer for all
options.then: He answers well. The others' parts go unmentioned.

options.text: Name each person's contribution to the rework
options.then: The professor writes each name. Your teammates stand a little taller.

steps.why: Crediting each person openly builds trust and lifts the whole team.

scenarios.debrief: Owning the outcome and rallying the fix is what marks you as a leader.
scenarios.relearn: Owning mistakes builds you as a leader; blaming the team undercuts it.

scenarios.hook: The fest committee offers you the lead on the inter-college fest stall, bigger than anything you've run.

steps.prompt: They need an answer by tomorrow. What do you do?

options.text: Say yes, and ask one mentor to check in with you
options.then: A faculty adviser agrees to mentor you. You sleep badly, but you start a list.

options.text: Decline, assuming you aren't ready for something this big
options.then: They give it to Kunal, who asks you to handle the stall design.

options.text: Say yes, and plan to handle everything alone
options.then: You take on everything, and the list grows by the day.

options.text: Ask for another week to think it over, then wait
options.then: They can't wait, so it goes to Kunal. He asks you to do the stall design.

steps.why: Saying yes, with light support, is a smart way into a bigger role.

steps.prompt: A week in, a committee member says your stall idea is too ambitious. What do you do?

options.text: Drop your idea and switch to a safer, older one
options.then: The stall looks like last year's. Nobody is excited.

options.text: Argue that he's wrong and carry on regardless
options.then: He shrugs, but help from his side of the team dries up.

options.text: Ask him to decide what the stall should be for you
options.then: He designs it. It's his stall now, not yours.

options.text: Ask what worries him, and keep the core idea
options.then: He names two risks. You fix them and keep the idea.

steps.why: Asking what worries him while keeping your idea shows you can lead and listen.

steps.prompt: With two days to go, you're exhausted and behind. What do you do?

options.text: Stay up for two nights to finish all of it yourself
options.then: The stall is ready. You're too tired to enjoy the opening.

options.text: Cut the stall down to bare basics and apologise
options.then: The stall looks thin, and the team wonders what happened.

options.text: Tell the team you're behind, and hand off two tasks
options.then: Two teammates take the signage and the cash box. You breathe.

options.text: Say nothing to anyone and hope it all works out
options.then: Two jobs fall through on the morning of the fest.

steps.why: Asking for help and sharing the work is part of leading, not a failure.

steps.prompt: After the fest, the committee asks you to lead the college's cultural week next term. What do you do?

options.text: Say no, since you think the fest was mostly luck
options.then: They shrug. The role goes to someone with less experience.

options.text: Say yes, and mention what you'd do differently
options.then: They nod, and you sketch your changes on a napkin.

options.text: Say yes, but only if everything stays the same
options.then: They agree. The same rough patches come back.

options.text: Say you'll decide after exams and let them know
options.then: Exams end, and somebody else has been named.

steps.why: A yes that names what you'd improve shows growth from the role.

scenarios.debrief: Stretch roles grow you. Pairing a yes with light support is a smart way in.
scenarios.relearn: Say yes to stretch leadership roles; you grow into them.

scenarios.hook: You're chairing the club meeting and three people have done all the talking for ten minutes.

steps.prompt: Others are shifting in their seats. What do you do?

options.text: Say, "I'd love to hear from those who haven't. Kabir?"
options.then: Kabir shares a plan nobody else had, and the room perks up.

options.text: Let the confident few keep steering a little longer
options.then: The meeting runs long, and two members check their phones.

options.text: Cut the three off sharply and say time is up
options.then: They go quiet, and the room turns stiff.

options.text: Move straight to a vote so the meeting finishes sooner
options.then: The vote follows the loud three, and the quiet ones stay out of it.

steps.why: Naming someone who hasn't spoken draws in voices a general invitation misses.

steps.prompt: Later Kabir says, "Um, I'm not sure about this," then trails off. What do you do?

options.text: Thank him and move straight on to the next person
options.then: The point is left hanging. Kabir sinks back into his chair.

options.text: Finish his point for him, to save everyone time
options.then: You get it partly wrong. Kabir nods, unsure.

options.text: Tell him to speak up more clearly next time
options.then: He flushes and says nothing more.

options.text: Say, "Go on. I'd like to hear where you're going."
options.then: Kabir straightens. "The budget doesn't cover the venue."

steps.why: A warm prompt gives him room to finish without putting him on the spot.

steps.prompt: On the next item, Kabir starts to speak, and a confident member cuts in with his own point. What do you do?

options.text: Let the member go ahead, since the meeting is long
options.then: He takes the floor, and Kabir fades out again.

options.text: Ask the two of them to sort it out after the meeting
options.then: They do, but the club never hears Kabir's point.

options.text: Say, "Hold on. Let Kabir finish his point first."
options.then: The member nods and waits. Kabir finishes.

options.text: Ignore it and check the time for the next item
options.then: The moment passes, and Kabir stays silent.

steps.why: Handing the floor back is quick and keeps the meeting fair.

steps.prompt: After the meeting, a confident member says you were too slow. What do you say?

options.text: Apologise and promise to run it faster next time
options.then: He nods, and the next meeting returns to the confident few.

options.text: Say hearing everyone makes the plan stronger
options.then: He thinks it over, and agrees to give it another meeting.

options.text: Tell him that he should learn a little patience
options.then: He frowns, and the talk ends stiffly.

options.text: Ask him if he wants to chair the next meeting
options.then: He laughs and says no, but his complaint isn't settled.

steps.why: Pointing to what hearing everyone adds shows why the room is worth the wait.

scenarios.debrief: Deliberately drawing out the quieter voices is what inclusive leaders do.
scenarios.relearn: As a leader, deliberately invite the quieter voices in.

scenarios.hook: A junior on your team is clearly capable but never puts herself forward for visible tasks.

steps.prompt: A client presentation needs a presenter. What do you do?

options.text: Offer her the slot, and say you'll back her on it
options.then: She hesitates, then nods. "Okay. If you'll sit in."

options.text: Give the slot to whoever seems most confident
options.then: A confident teammate takes it and does fine. She watches from the back again.

options.text: Assume she'd say no, and don't ask her
options.then: The slot goes elsewhere. She never learns it was on offer.

options.text: Present it yourself, since it's the safest option
options.then: You present well. She takes the notes again.

steps.why: A clear offer with backing makes it easier for a capable person to step forward.

steps.prompt: Weeks later, the manager puts her on a client presentation, and she tells you she might freeze. What do you do?

options.text: Tell her to just be confident and not overthink it
options.then: She nods, and feels worse.

options.text: Say you'll take over the whole thing if she freezes
options.then: She relaxes, and quietly plans for you to take over.

options.text: Suggest she pick a shorter slot this time instead
options.then: She agrees, relieved, and takes a shorter slot.

options.text: Offer a practice run, and agree a signal if she stalls
options.then: She smiles shakily. You practise twice over chai.

steps.why: A practice run and a simple signal make the stretch feel safe to try.

steps.prompt: On the day, she starts well but loses her place halfway. What do you do?

options.text: Step in and finish the presentation yourself
options.then: The client turns to you with questions. She sits down, silent.

options.text: Look down at your notes and let her recover alone
options.then: She stumbles through, and the pause feels very long.

options.text: Catch her eye and quietly cue her next point
options.then: She finds her place and carries on. The client nods.

options.text: Interrupt with a joke to cover the pause for her
options.then: The client laughs, and her thread is gone for good.

steps.why: A quiet cue helps her recover on her own, which builds her confidence.

steps.prompt: Afterwards, she says she isn't sure she's 'leadership material'. What do you say?

options.text: Say that she'll get there one day, with time
options.then: She smiles politely. Nothing changes in how she sees herself.

options.text: Name two things that worked and ask what's next
options.then: She counts them, surprised, and names a next slot.

options.text: Say that maybe leading just isn't for everyone
options.then: She nods and steps back.

options.text: Change the subject to lunch and move along
options.then: She laughs, but the doubt stays with her.

steps.why: Naming specific strengths helps her see leadership in what she already did.

scenarios.debrief: Encouraging a capable person into a bigger role is leadership in itself.
scenarios.relearn: Encouraging others into leadership is leadership in itself.

scenarios.hook: You're stuck on a project decision and don't know the answer. The team's waiting on you.

steps.prompt: They all look at you. What do you do?

options.text: Say you're not sure, and think it through together
options.then: A teammate offers two options, and the team starts weighing them.

options.text: Bluff a confident answer you're unsure about
options.then: The team follows it, and a small problem starts to grow.

options.text: Say you'll get back to them and then delay it
options.then: A day passes, and the team starts on a plan without you.

options.text: Hand the decision to the loudest person on the team
options.then: He decides quickly. A quieter teammate's caution goes unheard.

steps.why: Admitting doubt and thinking it through together builds trust.

steps.prompt: Soon after, Dia whispers that she sees a flaw in the plan but won't say it aloud. What do you do?

options.text: Ignore it, since the plan is already set
options.then: The flaw shows up a week later.

options.text: Push her to say it aloud to the team right now
options.then: She reddens and mumbles it, and the team half hears it.

options.text: Raise her doubt yourself without naming her
options.then: The team adjusts the plan. Nobody knows the catch was hers.

options.text: Ask how she'd like it raised, and offer to help
options.then: She thinks. "You say it, but say it was mine." The plan changes.

steps.why: Checking with her first lifts her voice without putting her on the spot.

steps.prompt: The team splits two ways on how to go forward. What do you do?

options.text: Put it to a quick vote and move on right away
options.then: The vote is close, and the losing side stays grumpy.

options.text: Pick the side taken by your closest friend
options.then: The decision is made. The other half of the team notices.

options.text: Lay out both sides and test the riskiest part first
options.then: A small test settles it, and the team is relieved.

options.text: Postpone it until somebody changes their mind
options.then: The deadline creeps closer with nothing decided.

steps.why: Testing the riskiest piece replaces arguing with evidence.

steps.prompt: A week on, the work shows a gap in a call you made early on. What do you say to the team?

options.text: Say the team must have misread what you meant
options.then: The team stares. They did exactly what you asked.

options.text: Say your early call had a gap, and thank them
options.then: The team nods. Trust in your calls goes up.

options.text: Say nothing about it and quietly fix the plan
options.then: The plan works, but your teammates wonder why you went quiet.

options.text: Say every plan has gaps, so it's no big deal
options.then: The team shrugs, and nobody checks the next call closely.

steps.why: Owning the gap openly builds more trust than hiding it.

steps.prompt: A week later, a newer member asks how you handle not knowing the answer. What do you say?

options.text: Say you admit it, ask for help, and decide together
options.then: She nods. "So it's not a weakness."

options.text: Say you just research overnight and then sound sure
options.then: She nods, and feels she must always hide her doubts.

options.text: Say you avoid such decisions when you can
options.then: She laughs, unsure whether you're joking.

options.text: Say you ask the seniors to decide
options.then: She nods, and does the same, and the team waits longer.

steps.why: Showing how you handle doubt teaches others that asking is part of leading.

scenarios.debrief: Asking for help and admitting doubt builds trust. It doesn't shrink you.
scenarios.relearn: Good leaders ask for help and admit doubt; it builds trust.

scenarios.hook: At a department presentation, a slide shows your data but only your name. Sana built it with you.

steps.prompt: You're called to the front, and the slide is on screen. What do you do?

options.text: Say, "Quick note. Sana built this analysis with me."
options.then: Sana looks up, surprised. The faculty nod.

options.text: Let it stand, since correcting it feels awkward
options.then: The faculty thank you. Sana stares at the floor.

options.text: Whisper to Sana to fix it on the slide later
options.then: Sana nods, and the talk goes ahead with your name only.

options.text: Mention Sana at the very end, in a quick aside
options.then: A few people miss it. The slide still says your name.

steps.why: Crediting her at once, in the room, is a clear sign of a leader.

steps.prompt: A faculty member emails asking for the full analysis and who to contact. What do you reply?

options.text: Reply with your name and offer to share the file
options.then: He writes back to you alone. Sana isn't mentioned.

options.text: Ask Sana to reply instead, since she did the maths
options.then: Sana replies. The faculty write back to her, and you fade from the thread.

options.text: Say you'll check who should reply and get back to him
options.then: The email sits for days, and he writes to you again.

options.text: Reply with both names and say who did what
options.then: Sana gets copied. Both of you are invited to a follow-up.

steps.why: Naming both people, and what each did, keeps credit honest.

steps.prompt: Sana sees the shared deck still shows only your name, and asks about it. What do you say?

options.text: Say it really isn't that big a deal to anyone
options.then: She nods stiffly, and the slide stays as it is.

options.text: Ask her to fix it herself, since she has the file
options.then: She does it, feeling she had to claim her own credit.

options.text: Apologise, and offer to correct the slide today
options.then: She relaxes. "Thanks. That means a lot."

options.text: Say that you'll be sure to credit her next time
options.then: She nods, but the slide still carries your name alone.

steps.why: A plain apology and a fix repair both the credit and the trust.

steps.prompt: The department asks for a one-page summary to share. What do you do?

options.text: Put your name first and Sana's as 'support'
options.then: Sana sees it and quietly says nothing.

options.text: List both names and a line on each person's role
options.then: The summary goes out. Sana's name is on it too.

options.text: Leave all names off and mention only the lab
options.then: The summary is shared, and nobody knows who to ask.

options.text: Ask the faculty which names they'd like to see on it
options.then: The faculty say, "Whoever did the work." The question comes back to you.

steps.why: Both names and roles make the credit clear to everyone who reads it.

scenarios.debrief: Crediting people openly in the room is one of the clearest leadership signals.
scenarios.relearn: Sharing credit openly builds you as a leader.

scenarios.hook: Your study group keeps going in circles with no decision. You're not the 'leader' of it.

steps.prompt: It's the third session without a plan. What do you do?

options.text: Propose one plan for a week and offer to write it up
options.then: Heads nod. "Send it tonight," says the topper.

options.text: Wait for the topper to take charge, sooner or later
options.then: He doesn't, and another hour goes by.

options.text: Skip the group sessions and study alone instead
options.then: You study well for a week, then rejoin. The group is still stuck.

options.text: Ask each person to bring their own separate plan
options.then: Five plans arrive, and the circle starts again.

steps.why: One concrete plan, with someone to write it up, breaks a stalemate.

steps.prompt: A few days later you share a draft plan, and someone objects that it leaves out a topic he cares about. What do you do?

options.text: Defend the plan as it is and say it's final
options.then: The objector goes quiet and stops turning up.

options.text: Drop the plan and start the discussion over
options.then: Two hours pass, and the group settles on a vaguer plan.

options.text: Tell him to go and write a plan of his own instead
options.then: He shrugs, and the group splits in two.

options.text: Add it to the plan and adjust the schedule
options.then: The group agrees to a revised plan in ten minutes.

steps.why: Absorbing a fair objection keeps the plan shared without losing momentum.

steps.prompt: A week on, half the group hasn't done the tasks. What do you do?

options.text: Say you'll just do their tasks as well as yours
options.then: You cover them. By Friday you're worn out.

options.text: Call out the ones who slacked in the group chat
options.then: Two people reply defensively, and the chat goes silent.

options.text: Ask what got in the way and reset one small task
options.then: Two people admit it was too big. You cut it in half.

options.text: Let it slide and see what happens next week
options.then: Next week the same thing happens.

steps.why: Asking what got in the way resets the task to something people can do.

steps.prompt: The topper says he'd like to take over the plan. What do you say?

options.text: Hand it all over and step away from the group
options.then: He runs it, but your ideas stop reaching the plan.

options.text: Say yes, share the notes, and stay involved
options.then: He thanks you, and the plan runs smoothly with both of you on it.

options.text: Say no, since it's your plan and you built it
options.then: He shrugs, and the group splits between you.

options.text: Give it up, but make it clear you're annoyed
options.then: The mood sours, and the group tiptoes around you.

steps.why: Sharing ownership keeps the plan alive and the group together.

scenarios.debrief: Breaking a stalemate with a concrete plan is leadership without a title.
scenarios.relearn: Leadership is initiative and lifting others; you can lead from any seat.

scenarios.hook: A team event goes wrong on the day when the speaker cancels at the last minute.

steps.prompt: You're the calmest one there, and the room is buzzing with worry. What do you do?

options.text: Calmly reassign roles: "Who can fill twenty minutes?"
options.then: Two people volunteer, and the room settles.

options.text: Say you're panicking too and wait for instructions
options.then: The worry spreads, and more people start to panic.

options.text: Keep phoning the speaker and pleading for him to come
options.then: His phone goes unanswered, and ten minutes pass.

options.text: Cancel the session and apologise to the guests
options.then: Some guests head for the door, and the team begs you to think again.

steps.why: Calm, clear direction steadies a team in a crisis.

steps.prompt: A volunteer says she can talk about her internship but is nervous. What do you do?

options.text: Tell her anyone can fill in for twenty minutes
options.then: She feels lighter, but not ready.

options.text: Say you'll ask someone more senior to speak instead
options.then: The senior isn't there, and ten more minutes are lost.

options.text: Ask her to go on stage without any notes at all
options.then: She agrees, looks pale, and stumbles at the start.

options.text: Thank her and offer to introduce her and sit nearby
options.then: She nods, and her hands stop shaking.

steps.why: Backing a nervous volunteer makes it possible for her to step in.

steps.prompt: A guest complains loudly about the delay. What do you do?

options.text: Ignore him and carry on until the session starts
options.then: He complains louder, and others listen.

options.text: Argue that the delay isn't your fault at all
options.then: He leans in, and the complaint grows.

options.text: Apologise briefly, share the new plan, and offer tea
options.then: He calms down and takes a seat.

options.text: Send another volunteer to deal with him instead
options.then: The volunteer fumbles and looks back at you for help.

steps.why: A short apology and a clear plan settle worried guests.

steps.prompt: The session goes well. The real speaker calls with an apology. What do you do?

options.text: Tell him sharply that he's ruined your event
options.then: He hangs up, and the relationship is over.

options.text: Thank him and ask about a new date together
options.then: He offers a new date, and you note it in the calendar.

options.text: Say it's fine, then never contact him again
options.then: The call ends, and the team never hears from him again.

options.text: Ask him to pay for the cost of the delay and hall
options.then: He refuses, and the call ends sourly.

steps.why: Staying steady after the crisis keeps doors open for next time.

steps.prompt: At the wrap-up, the team credits you for saving the day. What do you say?

options.text: Say it took everyone, and name who did what
options.then: The volunteer smiles, and the team laughs with relief.

options.text: Accept the credit, since you were the one leading
options.then: Some teammates exchange glances.

options.text: Say it was nothing and change the subject
options.then: The team stops clapping. Your volunteer's work isn't named.

options.text: Say you should have had a backup speaker ready
options.then: The team goes quiet, and the mood deflates.

steps.why: Sharing credit by name is how a calm leader finishes a crisis.

scenarios.debrief: Calm, clear direction in a crisis is leadership, and it can be quiet.
scenarios.relearn: Lead in your own style; quiet, steady leadership counts as much as loud.

scenarios.hook: A teammate proposes a risky idea that everyone is silently doubting. You think it has promise.

steps.prompt: The silence stretches. What do you do?

options.text: Back it, and suggest testing the riskiest part first
options.then: The teammate brightens. Two others offer to help run the test.

options.text: Stay neutral so you're not blamed if it fails
options.then: The silence drags on. The teammate decides to try a small version alone.

options.text: Say it's too risky, just to keep everyone happy
options.then: The idea is shelved, but the teammate tries a small version alone.

options.text: Suggest putting it off until the next term starts
options.then: The teammate shrugs, and tries a small version alone.

steps.why: Backing a good idea while making it safer to try lifts the person who raised it.

steps.prompt: The teammate's small test goes badly. What do you do?

options.text: Say you had your doubts about it all along
options.then: The teammate goes quiet, then runs a second test alone to prove it.

options.text: Quietly move on to something else without a word
options.then: Nobody mentions it. The teammate tries a second test alone.

options.text: Blame the teammate for not planning it enough
options.then: The teammate withdraws, and later reruns the test without you.

options.text: Ask what they learned and adjust the next test
options.then: The teammate lists two lessons, and the team plans a smaller second test.

steps.why: Treating a failed test as learning keeps people willing to try.

steps.prompt: The second test works. A senior asks who came up with the idea. What do you say?

options.text: Say it was a team effort and leave it there
options.then: The senior nods, and the teammate's name isn't mentioned.

options.text: Take the credit, since the senior asked you
options.then: The teammate hears it from across the room and says nothing.

options.text: Name the teammate as the one behind the idea
options.then: The senior turns to the teammate, who glows.

options.text: Say you can't remember who first suggested it
options.then: The senior shrugs. The idea has no name on it.

steps.why: Naming who came up with it is honest credit that lifts them.

scenarios.debrief: Backing a good idea and helping de-risk it is how leaders lift others.
scenarios.relearn: Lifting others' ideas and helping shape them is leadership.

scenarios.hook: You're coordinating a campus drive. Halfway, you realise you over-promised on the timeline.

steps.prompt: You're a week behind the date you promised. What do you do?

options.text: Hide the slip and push everyone to the old date
options.then: The team works frantic hours, and quality drops.

options.text: Tell the team early and share a realistic timeline
options.then: The team is surprised, then relieved, and helps you re-plan.

options.text: Quietly shift the dates in the plan and say nothing
options.then: Someone notices and asks why it changed.

options.text: Blame the college office for causing the delays
options.then: The team nods, but they know that wasn't the reason.

steps.why: Owning the misjudgement early, with a realistic plan, keeps the team with you.

steps.prompt: The volunteers are worn out, and one asks if the last two weeks were wasted. What do you say?

options.text: Say you misjudged, and explain what changes now
options.then: She nods. "Okay. That I can work with."

options.text: Tell her not to be so negative about it
options.then: She stiffens, and the others go quiet.

options.text: Say the problems came down to the team's slow pace
options.then: The team stiffens, and someone quietly leaves the chat.

options.text: Change the subject to the next task on the list
options.then: The question hangs unanswered. She stays silent after that.

steps.why: Plainly owning the mistake answers their frustration honestly.

steps.prompt: A teammate offers to take over the timeline. What do you do?

options.text: Refuse politely, since it's your drive to run
options.then: He shrugs. You carry everything alone.

options.text: Hand it all over and step away from the drive
options.then: He runs it, and you feel out of the loop.

options.text: Say you'll think about it, then drop the topic
options.then: The offer lapses, and he stops asking.

options.text: Say yes to sharing it and agree how to check in
options.then: You split the timeline and review it each Friday.

steps.why: Sharing the load, with clear check-ins, keeps the drive on track.

steps.prompt: The drive ends on time. A volunteer asks for feedback on the planning. What do you say?

options.text: Say it all went fine, so there's nothing to change
options.then: She nods. The next drive repeats the same timeline mistake.

options.text: Say she should have warned you about it earlier
options.then: She stiffens. "You never asked."

options.text: Share what you'd do differently, and ask what they saw
options.then: She names two things, and you add them to a notes file for next year.

options.text: Say you'll ask the committee for feedback instead
options.then: The committee is slow to reply, and the team's view is lost.

steps.why: Asking for feedback and noting lessons turns the stumble into better planning.

scenarios.debrief: Owning a misjudgement early and resetting honestly is what keeps a team with you.
scenarios.relearn: Owning your own mistakes builds you as a leader.

scenarios.hook: In a group of mostly seniors, you have a useful idea but feel too junior to say it.

steps.prompt: The conversation pauses. What do you do?

options.text: Hold it back until you've been here a lot longer
options.then: Someone else raises a similar idea and gets the credit.

options.text: Offer it, saying you're newer but have an idea
options.then: A senior says, "Go on." Others lean in.

options.text: Whisper the idea to the senior sitting beside you
options.then: He says he'll mention it, and later presents it as his.

options.text: Type it in the meeting chat and stay silent
options.then: It scrolls past, and nobody reads it.

steps.why: Saying it from the junior seat lets the room judge the idea, not your rank.

steps.prompt: At the next meeting the idea comes up, and a senior says, "Interesting, but we tried this before." What do you do?

options.text: Ask what happened, and say what you'd change
options.then: He describes the failure. You point to a fix, and he pauses.

options.text: Drop it and apologise for wasting their time
options.then: The room moves on, though one senior glances back at you.

options.text: Argue that they must have done it wrong before
options.then: The room stiffens, and the senior stops listening.

options.text: Say nothing and look down at your notes again
options.then: The moment passes, and the room moves to the next item.

steps.why: Asking what happened turns a dismissal into a real discussion.

steps.prompt: After the meeting, a senior says, "Good idea. Send me a note." What do you do?

options.text: Wait for a quieter week before you send the note
options.then: A month later, the idea feels stale.

options.text: Ask him to pitch it for you in the next meeting
options.then: He pitches it, and you watch from the side.

options.text: Forget it, since he might have been only polite
options.then: Nothing follows, and the idea goes unused.

options.text: Send a short note that evening, with your name on it
options.then: He forwards it with your name and one line of support.

steps.why: Sending it promptly under your name keeps the idea and the credit yours.

steps.prompt: A week later, a newer member asks how to speak up when you feel too junior. What do you say?

options.text: Say you just never feel nervous about it
options.then: She looks down. "I wish I felt that way."

options.text: Say it only works when you know the seniors well
options.then: She nods, and keeps her ideas to herself.

options.text: Say it gets easier each time, and tell her to try
options.then: She smiles. "Next meeting, then."

options.text: Say she should wait until she's more senior
options.then: She nods quietly, and the room loses her next idea.

steps.why: Sharing that it gets easier helps the next person step up.

scenarios.debrief: You can lead from the most junior seat just by contributing the idea.
scenarios.relearn: You can lead from any seat, no title required.

scenarios.hook: Your project finished well. In the wrap-up, the praise is all flowing to you.

steps.prompt: The lead thanks you by name for the whole result. What do you say?

options.text: Honestly, Riya's research carried this, and Tarun's design.
options.then: Riya grins and Tarun sits up. The lead turns to note their names down.

options.text: Smile and say thank you, then credit everyone by email later
options.then: The praise settles on you. The email goes out two days after the room has moved on.

options.text: Say "Just doing my job" and change the subject
options.then: The lead nods. Nobody hears what Riya or Tarun actually did.

options.text: Say the whole team was great, without naming anyone
options.then: People clap politely. The lead still ties the result to you.

steps.why: Naming the specific people puts credit where it was earned.

steps.prompt: A week later, a new task comes up and the lead asks who should run it. What do you do?

options.text: Suggest Riya lead it, and offer to back her
options.then: Riya looks surprised, then pleased. The lead agrees to try it.

options.text: Take it yourself, since you know the project best
options.then: The lead agrees. Riya and Tarun go back to supporting roles.

options.text: Say you're too busy and leave it open
options.then: The lead picks someone at random. The task starts without a plan.

options.text: Suggest Riya, but only if she asks for it herself
options.then: Riya never hears she was considered. The moment passes quietly.

steps.why: Offering a role to someone who earned it grows them and the team.

steps.prompt: Tarun says he's nervous about presenting the design to the client. What do you say?

options.text: Run it by me once. Then it's yours to present.
options.then: He runs it twice. On the day he presents and handles the client's questions.

options.text: I'll present it for you. Don't worry
options.then: Relief crosses his face. The client meets you, and Tarun stays in the background.

options.text: Everyone gets nervous. Just get through it
options.then: He nods, unconvinced, and goes quiet for the rest of the day.

options.text: Ask the lead to pick someone else
options.then: The lead agrees, and Tarun's design gets presented by a stranger to it.

steps.why: Backing him to present it himself lifts him without doing it for him.

scenarios.debrief: Naming the specific people behind the win is a leader making others bigger.
scenarios.relearn: Making others feel bigger, not smaller, is the best leadership.

scenarios.hook: A new committee has no chair. You'd be good at it but worry it'll look like grabbing power.

steps.prompt: The first meeting starts and nobody volunteers. What do you do?

options.text: Offer to coordinate, if the group is okay with it
options.then: A couple of people nod. "Sounds fine," says one. Nobody objects.

options.text: Wait to be asked, so you don't look pushy
options.then: The meeting ends with no chair. Two days later, a member asks you to coordinate after all.

options.text: Suggest the senior member takes it, to be safe
options.then: She declines, saying she's busy. The group looks back at you, and you agree to take it.

options.text: Start running the meeting without asking anyone
options.then: The meeting moves fast. A few people look unsure who agreed to this.

steps.why: Offering openly, with the group's consent, is initiative and not a power grab.

steps.prompt: A week later, you're drafting the agenda and two members want different priorities. What do you do?

options.text: Put both on the agenda and let the group decide
options.then: The group votes. Both members feel heard, even the one who loses.

options.text: Pick the one you think matters more
options.then: It saves time. The other member goes quiet for the rest of the meeting.

options.text: Drop both to avoid friction
options.then: The meeting is smooth and empty. Both members wonder why they came.

options.text: Ask them to settle it between themselves first
options.then: They trade messages for days. The agenda is still open on the day.

steps.why: Letting the group decide keeps you coordinating, not controlling.

steps.prompt: A member jokes that you're "power hungry" for taking the lead. What do you do?

options.text: Laugh, then ask if the group is happy with how it's going
options.then: Two people say yes. One suggests rotating the role each term, and you agree.

options.text: Ignore it and carry on exactly as before
options.then: The joke hangs there. You never find out if others feel the same.

options.text: Laugh along, then pull back from coordinating
options.then: The next agenda goes out late, and the committee slows down.

options.text: Offer to quit the role on the spot
options.then: The room goes awkward. Two members insist you stay.

steps.why: Checking in keeps the group's consent alive and answers the joke calmly.

scenarios.debrief: Offering to lead openly, with the group's consent, is taking initiative, not grabbing.
scenarios.relearn: Taking initiative when there's a gap is leadership.

scenarios.hook: You're running a workshop and one participant clearly knows more than you on a sub-topic.

steps.prompt: Dev corrects a detail you just gave, and he is right. What do you do?

options.text: Thank him, then ask him to take five minutes
options.then: Dev looks pleased and walks to the board. The room leans in.

options.text: Thank him and carry on with your slides
options.then: Dev sits back down. His knowledge stays with him for the rest of the session.

options.text: Say you'll check it later and move on
options.then: The room waits. A few people start checking their phones.

options.text: Talk over him to keep the room's attention
options.then: Dev stops mid-sentence. Several participants exchange glances.

steps.why: Handing the floor to real expertise makes the whole room better.

steps.prompt: Later, two participants debate a point you only half know. What do you do?

options.text: Say you're unsure and ask who can help
options.then: Two hands go up. The debate turns into a useful exchange.

options.text: Give your best guess in a confident tone
options.then: It sounds solid. One participant later finds it isn't.

options.text: Park it and promise an answer next week
options.then: The debate stops. The group leaves with it unresolved.

options.text: Shut it down to keep to the schedule
options.then: They stop mid-sentence. The energy in the room dips.

steps.why: Admitting what you don't know and using the room builds trust.

steps.prompt: At the end, the organiser asks who deserves credit for the session. What do you say?

options.text: Share it, naming Dev and the others
options.then: The organiser writes the names down. Dev smiles.

options.text: Take it, since you ran the session
options.then: The organiser thanks you alone. Dev says nothing.

options.text: Say it was all Dev's doing
options.then: The organiser nods. Your own planning goes unmentioned.

options.text: Say "it was a team thing" and leave it there
options.then: The organiser nods and moves on. No one's name is noted.

steps.why: Naming everyone, yourself included, is fair credit.

scenarios.debrief: Handing the floor to someone who knows more makes you the leader who lifts others.
scenarios.relearn: Lifting others up is a respected form of leadership.

scenarios.hook: You proposed a plan, but a teammate's counter-plan is clearly better.

steps.prompt: Anaya finishes presenting her counter-plan and the room turns to you. What do you say?

options.text: Say "Anaya's is better. Let's use it."
options.then: Anaya blinks, then smiles. The room relaxes and someone starts taking notes.

options.text: Defend your plan with a few solid points
options.then: The talk tightens into a debate. The group picks Anaya's plan anyway, and she looks tired.

options.text: Suggest a merge so your plan isn't lost
options.then: The merge takes an hour. It's mostly Anaya's, with your weaker parts bolted on.

options.text: Say you'll think about it and decide later
options.then: The meeting ends unresolved. Two days later, the group settles on Anaya's plan without you.

steps.why: Backing the stronger plan puts the goal ahead of ego.

steps.prompt: A week into Anaya's plan, the work hits a snag. What do you do?

options.text: Tell the group plainly and ask what each person sees
options.then: Three people offer fixes. The snag becomes a short list.

options.text: Fix it quietly yourself so it doesn't spread
options.then: It works out overnight. The group only hears about it later.

options.text: Mention it wasn't the plan you'd have picked
options.then: A few people shift in their seats. The mood sours.

options.text: Wait for Anaya to raise it first
options.then: Days pass. The snag grows while each waits on the other.

steps.why: Raising problems openly and asking for input builds shared ownership.

steps.prompt: The client praises the result and asks who led. What do you say?

options.text: Name Anaya for the plan and the group for the work
options.then: The client nods. Anaya looks over, surprised and glad.

options.text: Say you led, since you set up the project
options.then: The client thanks you. Anaya stares at her notes.

options.text: Say "a group effort" and stop there
options.then: The client smiles and moves on. No one is named.

options.text: Mention Anaya's plan, then add that yours was the base
options.then: The client nods. Anaya looks a little deflated.

steps.why: Naming who shaped the result is how a leader shares credit.

scenarios.debrief: Backing the better idea over your own ego is exactly what trustworthy leaders do.
scenarios.relearn: Sharing credit and backing the best idea builds you as a leader.

scenarios.hook: A teammate freezes mid-presentation in front of the panel. You're sitting beside them.

steps.prompt: Kabir goes silent mid-slide and the panel waits. What do you do?

options.text: Pick up the thread: "To add to that point..."
options.then: You cover smoothly. Kabir breathes out and finds his place again.

options.text: Let the silence hang so he sorts it out alone
options.then: The silence drags. Kabir stares at his slide and loses the thread further.

options.text: Whisper the next line to him
options.then: He mumbles it, flustered. The panel glances between you two.

options.text: Take over the rest of the presentation
options.then: You finish his slides. Kabir sits down, embarrassed.

steps.why: Bridging the gap briefly lets him recover without taking over.

steps.prompt: After the panel, Kabir avoids your eye. What do you do?

options.text: Say it happens to many people, and ask how he is
options.then: He exhales. "I thought everyone noticed. Thanks for not making it weird."

options.text: Say nothing so you don't embarrass him more
options.then: Kabir keeps avoiding you. He assumes you're judging him.

options.text: Tell him it was fine and move on to lunch plans
options.then: He nods and goes along. The knot in his stomach stays.

options.text: Tell him he should have prepared more
options.then: His jaw tightens. "I did prepare." He walks off.

steps.why: Normalising it and asking how he is lets him talk about it.

steps.prompt: A week later, Kabir says he might skip the next presentation. What do you say?

options.text: Offer to rehearse with him and agree a signal for stalls
options.then: He agrees. "A signal would actually help."

options.text: Tell him skipping is fine if he's not comfortable
options.then: He relaxes. The team quietly gives his slot to someone else.

options.text: Tell him to just push through it
options.then: He goes pale. "Easy to say."

options.text: Offer to present his part for him
options.then: He accepts too fast. His part is now yours.

steps.why: Rehearsing together and planning a signal builds his confidence.

scenarios.debrief: Quietly covering for a stumbling teammate is leadership that lifts others.
scenarios.relearn: Lifting and supporting others is a powerful form of leadership.

scenarios.hook: You can run a project the "usual loud" way, or in your own quieter, methodical style.

steps.prompt: The team expects a big kickoff speech from you as the new lead. What do you do?

options.text: Share clear notes and book a short check-in with each person
options.then: The plan is on paper by evening. People know who owns what.

options.text: Give a loud, high-energy speech like the last lead did
options.then: The room claps. You spend the evening drained and unsure what you promised.

options.text: Skip the kickoff and let people start on their own
options.then: People head in different directions. By Friday nobody knows who owns what.

options.text: Ask the last lead to run the kickoff for you
options.then: He does, and the team treats him as the lead. You're left in the background.

steps.why: Clear notes and one-to-one check-ins are a real leadership style, and it's yours.

steps.prompt: Two weeks in, a teammate says she wishes you'd speak up more in meetings. What do you do?

options.text: Thank her, and ask what she'd like to hear from you
options.then: She names two things: deadlines and decisions. You add both to your notes.

options.text: Promise to be louder from next week
options.then: You try. By the third meeting you feel fake and go quiet again.

options.text: Explain that loud isn't your style and end the talk
options.then: She nods politely. She stops giving you feedback.

options.text: Ask the team to adjust to how you lead
options.then: A few shrug. Others say they'll try, but nothing concrete is agreed.

steps.why: Asking what she needs lets you adapt without dropping your own style.

steps.prompt: Deadline pressure builds and two people start to clash in meetings. What do you do?

options.text: Meet each alone, then agree a written plan
options.then: Both feel heard. The written plan settles who does what.

options.text: Speak over them to stop the argument
options.then: The room goes silent. The disagreement goes underground.

options.text: Send a long email telling both to cooperate
options.then: Both reply politely. Neither changes anything.

options.text: Let them fight it out so the stronger idea wins
options.then: The louder of the two wins. The quieter one stops offering ideas.

steps.why: One-to-one talks and a written plan suit a methodical style and settle things.

scenarios.debrief: Leading in your own style beats imitating one that isn't you.
scenarios.relearn: Lead in your own style; quiet leadership counts as much as loud.

scenarios.hook: A capable teammate keeps underselling her work in the team chat.
scenarios.setup: Pooja has just posted her analysis.

steps.prompt: Pooja writes: "Sorry, this is probably rubbish, but here's the analysis."

options.text: "This analysis is sharp. You should present it."
options.then: Pooja replies after a pause. "Really? Okay."

options.text: "Thanks for sharing. I'll go through it tonight."
options.then: Pooja sends a thumbs-up. Her apology stands in the chat, unanswered.

options.text: "Stop saying sorry. It's annoying."
options.then: Pooja goes offline. Nobody else replies.

options.text: "I can present it, if you'd rather not."
options.then: Pooja types: "Oh. Okay, if you think that's best." Her next message is another apology.

steps.why: Naming what's strong and asking her to present lifts her directly.

steps.prompt: A day later, Pooja messages you: "I never know if my work is good enough."

options.text: "It's good. Want to go through the parts you're unsure of?"
options.then: Pooja sends three points. You talk them through and she sounds steadier.

options.text: "Everyone feels that way. Don't overthink it."
options.then: Pooja sends a smile. She still doesn't know where she stands.

options.text: "Then ask the lead to check it before you share."
options.then: She agrees. It adds a day, and she still doubts herself.

options.text: "You'd do better if you tried harder."
options.then: Pooja stops replying. The message sits read.

steps.why: Specific feedback shows her what's strong, which general comfort can't.

steps.prompt: The lead writes in the chat: "Who wants to present the analysis at the review?"

options.text: "Pooja built it. She should present it."
options.then: Pooja types: "Okay. I'll do it." You offer to rehearse with her.

options.text: "I'll do it. I know the numbers too."
options.then: The lead adds your name. Pooja stays quiet.

options.text: "Happy to. Pooja can answer questions if they come."
options.then: The lead agrees. Pooja is cast as the helper on her own work.

options.text: "I'm not sure who's best. Anyone else?"
options.then: Two minutes pass. The lead picks whoever replies first.

steps.why: Naming her as the owner puts her in front of her own work.

scenarios.relearn: Lifting others by naming their strengths is a generous form of leadership.

scenarios.hook: You over-committed your team to a deadline you now know is too tight.
scenarios.setup: The team is already working toward it.

steps.prompt: Dhruv says: "We're going to miss Friday. Did you know this was tight?"

options.text: "That was my call. Let's reset it together."
options.then: Dhruv lets out a breath. "Okay. Thanks for saying so."

options.text: "We can still make it if everyone pushes hard."
options.then: Dhruv sighs. "We've been pushing already."

options.text: "The client pushed for that date."
options.then: Dhruv raises an eyebrow. "You agreed to it."

options.text: "Let's see how far we get first."
options.then: Dhruv frowns. Nobody tells the client, and the days tick by.

steps.why: Owning the misjudgement early lets the team reset the plan together.

steps.prompt: A day later, Dhruv asks: "So what do we tell the client about Friday?"

options.text: "I'll call them and propose a new date with a plan."
options.then: Dhruv nods. "Want me to send you the task list?"

options.text: "Tell them things are on track for now."
options.then: Dhruv hesitates. "Until when?"

options.text: "Let's wait until Thursday before we tell them."
options.then: Dhruv shakes his head. "That's one day's notice."

options.text: "You explain it. You know the tasks best."
options.then: He looks uneasy. "I'd rather you did. It was your call."

steps.why: Facing the client yourself, with a plan, is what ownership means.

steps.prompt: Dhruv asks: "Next time, how do we avoid this?"

options.text: "I'll check dates with you before I promise them."
options.then: Dhruv smiles. "That would help a lot."

options.text: "I'll just set longer deadlines from now on to be safe."
options.then: Dhruv laughs. "Everything will look slow."

options.text: "You should flag things earlier."
options.then: Dhruv bristles. "I did flag it. You didn't ask."

options.text: "Let's not go over it again. It's done."
options.then: Dhruv nods. He won't flag things next time.

steps.why: Checking with the team before committing turns the slip into a better habit.

scenarios.relearn: Owning your own mistake early builds trust; hiding it erodes it.

scenarios.hook: You're unsure how to solve a problem your team is looking to you for.
scenarios.setup: The group has stopped and turned to you.

steps.prompt: Nisha says: "Okay, what's the plan? You'll know how to fix this."

options.text: "Not solved yet. Let's crack it together."
options.then: Nisha sits forward. "Okay. I have one thought already."

options.text: "I'll have a plan by tomorrow. Give me a bit."
options.then: Nisha nods. You spend the night guessing while the team waits.

options.text: "Try the approach we used last time."
options.then: Nisha frowns. "That was a different problem."

options.text: "Good question. What does everyone else think?"
options.then: Nisha blinks. "You were meant to know." The room goes awkward.

steps.why: Saying you haven't solved it yet, and inviting the team in, builds trust.

steps.prompt: Nisha says: "Honestly, I thought leads always had the answers."

options.text: "I don't need every answer. You each know a piece."
options.then: Nisha sits up. "Well, I know the data side." Others start sharing.

options.text: "I usually do. This one's just unusual."
options.then: Nisha nods, but the team still waits on you.

options.text: "Don't worry. I'll work it out on my own by tomorrow."
options.then: You go home to work alone. The team disperses.

options.text: "Right, enough talk. Let's move on."
options.then: The room stiffens. The problem is still unsolved.

steps.why: Admitting you don't hold every answer brings the team's knowledge in.

steps.prompt: Nisha offers: "What if we cut step three and test it early?"

options.text: "I like that. Let's test it and see."
options.then: Nisha grins. You try it that afternoon, and the first results show a path.

options.text: "Hmm, not sure. Let's stick with the old way."
options.then: Nisha shrinks back. The group goes quiet.

options.text: "Good idea. I'll take it from here."
options.then: Nisha's face drops. The fix becomes yours.

options.text: "I can't tell if that works. Let me think alone first."
options.then: Nisha nods, but the group waits another day.

steps.why: Testing her idea keeps the group moving and credits her.

scenarios.relearn: Good leaders ask for help and admit doubt; it builds trust.

scenarios.hook: A quieter teammate hasn't spoken in the whole planning meeting.
scenarios.setup: The meeting is nearly over.

steps.prompt: Meera says: "Great, so we're agreed. Shall we wrap up?"

options.text: "Nikhil, you've been thinking. What's your read?"
options.then: Nikhil looks up. "Actually, yes." His point on the budget changes the plan.

options.text: "Sounds agreed. Let's wrap up."
options.then: The meeting ends. Nikhil closes his laptop without a word.

options.text: "Anyone else? Last chance before we close."
options.then: Nobody speaks. Nikhil looks at his notes, and Meera wraps up.

options.text: "I'll message Nikhil for his view afterwards."
options.then: The meeting ends. Nikhil replies later with one short line.

steps.why: A warm, specific invitation gives him a real opening to speak.

steps.prompt: The next day, Nikhil says: "Something about the timeline bothers me, but it's probably nothing."

options.text: "It might matter. Tell me what you noticed."
options.then: Nikhil describes a clash with another team's deadline. "I hadn't seen that," you say.

options.text: "If it's nothing, let's skip it."
options.then: Nikhil nods. The clash surfaces a month later.

options.text: "Write it up and send it to everyone."
options.then: Nikhil sighs. He writes nothing.

options.text: "Thanks for telling me. I'll take it from here."
options.then: Nikhil shrugs. The worry is now yours, not his.

steps.why: Treating his worry as worth hearing shows him his view matters.

steps.prompt: Nikhil asks: "Should I speak up more in the big meetings?"

options.text: "I'll make room. Want to pick a point beforehand?"
options.then: He smiles. "Okay. I'd like that."

options.text: "Yes. You need to be louder to be heard here."
options.then: Nikhil nods slowly, deflated.

options.text: "No, you're fine as you are. Don't change anything."
options.then: He relaxes. Nothing changes in the next meeting.

options.text: "Just copy how Meera does it in meetings."
options.then: "I'm not her," he says.

steps.why: Making room and planning a point gives him a way in on his own terms.

scenarios.relearn: Deliberately inviting quieter voices in is inclusive leadership.

scenarios.hook: You've never led anything this big, and you feel underqualified.
scenarios.setup: Your mentor, Mrs Rao, calls you into her office.

steps.prompt: Mrs Rao says: "We'd like you to lead the new student drive. Will you take it?"

options.text: "I'd like to take it. I'll learn fast and ask for help."
options.then: Mrs Rao smiles. "Good. I'll send you the details."

options.text: "I'm probably not ready. Give it to someone else."
options.then: Mrs Rao nods. "Sleep on it." You say yes two days later, still unsure.

options.text: "Can I take a month to think?"
options.then: Mrs Rao smiles, a little tight. "We need a name by Friday." You say yes.

options.text: "Only if someone more senior co-leads with me."
options.then: Mrs Rao frowns. "That changes the role." She agrees to a trial run.

steps.why: Saying yes to a stretch role, with a plan to learn, is how you grow into it.

steps.prompt: Days later, your senior teammate Kabir says: "No offence, but I thought I'd be leading this."

options.text: "I hear you. Could you take the budget side?"
options.then: Kabir sits up. "I'd like that. I know the numbers."

options.text: "You're right. Maybe you should lead it."
options.then: Kabir hesitates. "That's not what I meant."

options.text: "Mrs Rao offered it to me, so that's settled."
options.then: Kabir's jaw tightens. He stops sharing ideas.

options.text: "Sorry. I'll try not to get in your way."
options.then: Kabir looks awkward. "You're not in my way."

steps.why: Hearing him and giving him a real part keeps you leading and includes him.

steps.prompt: Weeks later, Mrs Rao asks: "I heard the venue fell through. What happened?"

options.text: "I missed a confirmation. Here's the new plan."
options.then: Mrs Rao nods. "Thanks for telling me straight. Let's look at it."

options.text: "It fell through, but the venue was unreliable."
options.then: Mrs Rao raises an eyebrow. "And the confirmation?"

options.text: "I'm not cut out for this. I should step back."
options.then: Mrs Rao shakes her head. The plan is still missing.

options.text: "Kabir was meant to confirm it."
options.then: Mrs Rao goes quiet. Kabir hears about it by evening.

steps.why: Owning the slip and bringing a plan is what earns trust in a new role.

scenarios.relearn: Say yes to stretch roles; you grow into them.

scenarios.hook: In the wrap-up, the credit for a win is landing only on you.
scenarios.setup: The director is congratulating you in front of everyone.

steps.prompt: The director says: "Wonderful result. This was all your doing."

options.text: "It was a team effort. Anaya's idea turned it."
options.then: The director turns to Anaya. "Tell me more about that."

options.text: "Thank you. I'm glad it worked out."
options.then: The director beams. Anaya looks at her notebook.

options.text: "Thanks. I did put in long hours on this."
options.then: The director nods warmly. The hours become the story.

options.text: "I'd rather not take credit. It was just luck."
options.then: The director looks puzzled. "Luck? No, you led it."

steps.why: Naming the person behind the turning point shares credit where it belongs.

steps.prompt: Later, Anaya says quietly: "I'm not sure how much my part mattered."

options.text: "It mattered a lot. The whole plan turned on it."
options.then: Anaya smiles. "Thanks. I wasn't sure anyone saw that."

options.text: "Don't worry. Credit doesn't matter much anyway."
options.then: Anaya nods, but her shoulders drop.

options.text: "You can tell the director yourself if it bothers you."
options.then: Anaya looks away. "It's not that easy for me."

options.text: "It mattered. I'll tell the director how much."
options.then: Anaya shrugs. "Okay." She'd rather have said it herself.

steps.why: Telling her plainly what her part did lets her hear it and own it.

steps.prompt: The director asks: "Whom would you put forward to lead the next project?"

options.text: "Anaya. Her idea drove the result. She's ready."
options.then: The director writes the name down. "I'll ask her."

options.text: "Me, since I know the client."
options.then: The director nods. Anaya hears about it from others.

options.text: "I'd have to think about who's suited."
options.then: The director waits, then picks someone else.

options.text: "Anaya, but she may not want the pressure."
options.then: The director nods. "Maybe. I'll see who puts their hand up."

steps.why: Naming her outright turns credit into a real opening.

scenarios.relearn: Sharing credit and naming people builds you as a leader.

scenarios.hook: A capable friend keeps saying she's "not leadership material" before a club election.
scenarios.setup: Tara is looking at the nomination form.

steps.prompt: Tara says: "I'm not leadership material. Let someone else stand."

options.text: "You'd be great. Stand for it. I'll back you."
options.then: Tara looks up. "You'd really back me?"

options.text: "Maybe it's safer to sit this one out this time."
options.then: Tara nods, relieved. The blank form is still in her hand by the end of lunch.

options.text: "Who do you think should stand, then?"
options.then: Tara names someone else and sounds glad to step aside. She keeps the form anyway.

options.text: "You do talk less than the others."
options.then: Tara laughs thinly. "Right." She keeps the form anyway.

steps.why: Saying she'd be great and you'll back her is the push she needs.

steps.prompt: Tara asks: "What would I even say if people ask why I want it?"

options.text: "Say what you'd change and why it matters to you."
options.then: Tara thinks. "Better seating, and a real budget. That's true."

options.text: "Say you just want to help out. It's a safe line."
options.then: Tara nods. It sounds flat, and she knows it.

options.text: "Copy what Rohan said last year."
options.then: "It won't sound like me," Tara says.

options.text: "Tell them honestly that you're not sure you'll win."
options.then: Tara winces. "That would put me off too."

steps.why: Her own reasons sound stronger than a safe line.

steps.prompt: The night before, Tara texts: "I'm having second thoughts. Everyone else seems so sure."

options.text: "Nervous is normal. Want to run your pitch past me?"
options.then: Tara sends a voice note. "Okay. Here goes." You hear the whole pitch.

options.text: "You can always pull out if it feels too much."
options.then: Tara replies with a thumbs-up, unconvinced.

options.text: "Everyone else is faking it. Ignore them."
options.then: Tara doesn't reply for an hour.

options.text: "You'll win. I'm sure of it."
options.then: Tara sends a nervous emoji. She now fears letting you down.

steps.why: Normalising nerves and offering to listen helps more than a promise.

scenarios.relearn: Encouraging others into leadership is leadership in itself.

scenarios.hook: Nobody's stepping up to coordinate a stalled group assignment.
scenarios.setup: It's three days before the deadline and the chat has gone quiet.

steps.prompt: Raj writes in the group chat: "Is anyone coordinating this? We're stuck."

options.text: "I'll split the steps. Shout if you want a different bit."
options.then: Raj replies: "Finally. Send it over."

options.text: "Maybe the professor can tell us who's leading."
options.then: Raj replies: "That'll take days."

options.text: "Someone senior will probably step up."
options.then: Raj sends a shrug. Nobody does.

options.text: "I'll just do all of it myself. It's quicker."
options.then: Raj sends a thumbs-up. By midnight you hold everyone's work.

steps.why: Taking initiative with a clear split and an open door leads without taking over.

steps.prompt: The next day, Isha writes: "I can take on more. What should I do?"

options.text: "Take the research part. I'll send the outline now."
options.then: Isha sends a thumbs-up. The outline goes out within the hour.

options.text: "Whatever you like. I don't mind."
options.then: Isha waits, then picks something that overlaps with Raj.

options.text: "Wait for the others to reply first."
options.then: Isha waits. The chat stays quiet for a day.

options.text: "Tell me what you're good at. I'll decide later."
options.then: Isha sends a long list. The decision sits with you for days.

steps.why: Giving a clear piece of work quickly keeps everyone moving.

steps.prompt: Raj writes: "Some of the work is thin. Should we tell the professor we need more time?"

options.text: "Let's fix the weakest parts first, then decide."
options.then: Raj agrees. Two hours on, the gaps are clear and small.

options.text: "Yes. Ask for a week so we can relax."
options.then: Raj sends the email. The professor says one day, not a week.

options.text: "No. Submit as it is and hope for the best."
options.then: Raj hesitates. The work goes in as it is.

options.text: "Let's ask Isha to redo the thin parts alone."
options.then: Isha goes quiet. She now carries the weakest work alone.

steps.why: Checking the weak spots first keeps the decision honest and shared.

Re-proving themselves each time is the 'prove-it-again' bias, not weaker skill.
scenarios.hook: "If she keeps having to re-prove herself, maybe she's just not that good."

myth.un: If she keeps having to re-prove herself, she's probably not that good.
myth.re: Being asked to prove it again and again is a known bias; the same proof is taken on trust from others.
myth.why: The repeated burden is the bias, not a sign of weaker skill.

scenarios.relearn: Disliking a woman for the same confidence we admire in a man is the likeability bias.
scenarios.hook: "She's good at the job, I just find her a bit much."

myth.un: She's competent, I just find her a bit much.
myth.re: Liking a confident man but finding the same woman 'a bit much' is the likeability bias talking.
myth.why: The discomfort tracks her gender, not her actual behaviour.

scenarios.relearn: Crediting her wins to luck or the team, his to skill, is attribution bias.
scenarios.hook: "She got the deal: good luck and a strong team. He got his on pure skill."

myth.un: Her win was luck and the team; his was pure skill.
myth.re: Putting her success down to luck or others, and his to ability, is attribution bias.
myth.why: The same result gets read as skill for him, fluke for her.

scenarios.relearn: Feedback that polices a woman's tone instead of her work is gendered, not helpful.
scenarios.hook: "Her review said 'abrasive' and 'too aggressive' but nothing about the actual work."

myth.un: 'Abrasive' and 'too aggressive' is fair feedback on her.
myth.re: Reviews that police a woman's tone while skipping her results are gendered feedback.
myth.why: Men with the same style get called direct, not abrasive.

scenarios.relearn: Telling a woman to smile or soften is tone-policing, not professional advice.
scenarios.hook: "Someone told her she'd go further if she just smiled more."

myth.un: She'd go further if she smiled more and softened up.
myth.re: Telling a woman to smile or soften, while never saying it to men, is tone-policing.
myth.why: Her face and warmth aren't the job; the advice only flows one way.

scenarios.relearn: Skipping a mother for a stretch role 'for her own good' is the motherhood penalty.
scenarios.hook: "Don't give her the big project: she's a new mum, she won't want the pressure."

myth.un: Don't offer her the stretch role; as a new mum she won't want it.
myth.re: Deciding for a mother that she can't handle big work is the motherhood penalty: ask, don't assume.
myth.why: Assuming her choices for her quietly sidelines her career.

scenarios.relearn: Calling a qualified woman a 'diversity hire' erases her merit; it's a bias, not a fact.
scenarios.hook: "She only got in because they needed more women, a diversity hire."

myth.un: She only got the role to fill a women's quota.
myth.re: Branding a qualified woman a 'diversity hire' erases the merit that got her in.
myth.why: It assumes she couldn't have earned it, which is the bias.

scenarios.relearn: A woman's idea ignored, then praised from a man, is 'hepeating': re-credit her.
scenarios.hook: "Her idea got nothing; he said it ten minutes later and the room loved it."

myth.un: If her idea only landed when he said it, it wasn't ready when she did.
myth.re: An idea ignored from her, then praised from a man, is 'hepeating': same idea, different messenger.
myth.why: The room rewarded the speaker's gender, not the idea's timing.

scenarios.relearn: 'Protecting' a woman out of hard work is benevolent sexism; let her choose.
scenarios.hook: "I didn't send her to the tough client site. I was protecting her."

myth.un: Keeping her off the tough assignment was me protecting her.
myth.re: 'Protecting' a woman out of demanding work is benevolent sexism; it still costs her the chance.
myth.why: Kindly-meant gatekeeping is still gatekeeping.

scenarios.relearn: Asking only women about marriage plans in interviews is biased and off-limits.
scenarios.hook: "In my interview they asked when I plan to marry, never asked the men."

myth.un: Asking a woman candidate about marriage plans is just normal small talk.
myth.re: Quizzing only women on marriage or kids in hiring is bias. It judges her on a future, not the work.
myth.why: It treats her life plans as a risk it never weighs for men.

scenarios.relearn: A woman seen as competent OR likeable, rarely both, is the double-bind, not reality.
scenarios.hook: "Warm women seem soft; tough women seem cold. Can't she just be both?"

myth.un: A woman is either warm or tough; she can't really be both.
myth.re: Being forced to choose warm-but-weak or strong-but-cold is the double-bind women face, not a real limit.
myth.why: Men are allowed to be both at once; the trap is the bias.

scenarios.relearn: Handing women leadership only in a crisis sets them up to fail: the 'glass cliff'.
scenarios.hook: "They finally made her head of the failing division nobody else wanted."

myth.un: She got the top job, so the bias clearly didn't touch her.
myth.re: Promoting women mainly into failing units they're likely to be blamed for is the 'glass cliff'.
myth.why: The title comes with the highest chance of falling, by design.

options.text: "Maybe you misread it. Some people are just friendly."
options.then: Ritu doubts herself, but she doesn't leave.

options.text: "It's not really my place to get involved."
options.then: Ritu looks deflated, but stays where she is. She has no route yet.

options.text: "Tell me exactly what he said, word for word."

options.text: "It's better to settle it with him quietly."
options.then: Ritu looks frightened. "Alone?"

options.text: "Wait until your internship ends."
options.then: Ritu nods. The comments go on.

options.text: "Let's wait until you're completely sure."
